sens: son of Mattathias in the genealogy of Jesus in Luke
G0301G.detail: 1. Amos is an ancestor of Jesus mentioned in the genealogy provided by Luke in chapter 3. He is the son of Mattathias and the father of Nahum. This genealogy traces back from Jesus to Adam, showing how the Lord is woven into the history of God's people through a long chain of generations (Luke 3:25).
G0301G.origine: The name Amos comes from the Hebrew עָמוֹס (amôs), which means "to carry" or "to support." It is a common name in Israel. Do not confuse it with the prophet Amos, the author of the book of the same name, who lived several centuries earlier. In Luke's genealogy, this name designates a simple link in the lineage of David through which the Messiah was to come.
G0301G.emploi: Amos appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 3:25, in the genealogy of Jesus. Luke lists about seventy generations to show that Jesus is a descendant of David according to the promise made to his people. Amos is just a step in this journey, with no particular story attached to his name in the New Testament.

sens: King of Judah, son of Manasseh
G0301H.detail: Amon is a king of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus reported by Matthew. He is the son of King Manasseh and the father of King Josiah (Matthew 1:10).
G0301H.origine: The Hebrew name אָמוֹן (Amôn) likely means "faithful" or "artisan." In the Bible, this name also carries the idea of stability and assurance. The same name in Hebrew can refer to an Egyptian god, which may reflect the period of religious syncretism in the Near East.
G0301H.emploi: Amon appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:10, in the list of ancestors of Jesus. This enumeration of the kings of Judah emphasizes that Jesus comes from a royal lineage and that the history of Israel culminates in him, despite the unfaithfulness of past kings. Amon himself was a king in the 7th century BC, son of Manasseh and father of Josiah.
G0301H.portee: The mention of Amon in the genealogy of Jesus reminds us that God does not reject repentant sinners: although several kings of Judah committed unfaithfulness, the divine promise has endured and was fulfilled in Jesus Christ. This inclusion also shows that Jesus truly fits into the history of the Jewish people.

sens: Marks an unreal condition: what would happen or would have happened under certain circumstances
Introduces a general supposition or a rule applicable to all
Expresses a conditional or hypothetical consequence
Marks the time at which an action occurs or a condition is fulfilled
Adds to questions or wishes to express a possibility
G0302.detail:
1. In a sentence with apodosis (the consequence), ἄν indicates that the result depends on a condition: "If they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord" (1 Corinthians 2:8) — this is what *would have happened* if the condition had been met. This particle gives the sentence its unreal or hypothetical character.
2. With general words (ὃς ἄν = "whoever", ὅσοι ἄν = "all those who"), it indicates a rule valid for all similar cases: "Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it" (Luke 17:33) means: this applies to every person who acts this way.
3. With expressions of time (ἕως ἄν = "until", "as long as"), it shows when something ends or is fulfilled: "Until I speak to you" (Matthew 2:13) — the flight must last until the moment God speaks.
4. Sometimes ἄν combines with other particles (ὅταν, ἐπάν) to weave the condition directly into the temporal expression, obviously from the purest ancient Greek.
5. Before a question or a wish, it adds a nuance of potentiality: "Could you explain this to me?" — this is not a dry request, but a hypothesis of possibility.
G0302.origine: ἄν comes from ancient Greek and serves to mark unreality or generality. It is a pure grammatical tool: the particle itself has no concrete image, but it functions as a modifier that changes the meaning of other words. It attaches to verbs, pronouns (ὃς ἄν, ὅσοι ἄν) or conjunctions (εἰ ἄν = ἐάν) to nuance their meaning. Often, French cannot translate it separately: it must be integrated into the sentence through phrases like "if", "whoever", "until".
G0302.emploi: ἄν appears 165 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and the Epistles of Paul. It serves to express unreal conditions ("If you had been there...", John 11:32 implicit), general rules ("Whoever believes...", John 3:16 implicit), and temporal boundaries ("Until the Son of Man comes", Matthew 24:34 implicit). Jesus often uses it to express spiritual realities in the form of suppositions or general cases, giving his teaching a universal force: it applies to all, everywhere, always. Its absence or presence sometimes subtly changes the tone of a statement.
G0302.portee: This tiny particle is a precise theological instrument. It allows Jesus and the apostles to express divine conditions without rigidity: "If you ask anything in my name, I will do it" (John 14:14 implicit) does not say it is *mechanical*, but that it is *a reality that occurs* under this condition. For the reader, it teaches that God's will is never arbitrary, but always linked to conditions: faith, obedience, perseverance. It is an invitation to take the logic of the Kingdom seriously.

sens: Individually, one by one, apiece
In turn, alternately
In the midst of, among
Around
G0303.detail:
1. The most common meaning: each element of a group receives or does something individually. In Matthew 20:9-10, the workers receive "each one a denarius" — not a global share, but a distribution where each person gets their part. This is the idea of distinction within a whole.
2. Sometimes the word marks succession: in 1 Corinthians 14:27, those who speak in tongues must do so "each in turn," meaning one after another, in order. The emphasis is then on regular alternation.
3. In certain contexts, "ana" constructs an image of movement or distribution "among" or "through." In Mark 7:31, Jesus travels through the region of the Decapolis passing through the areas.
4. In Revelation 4:8, the four living creatures have "each six wings" — it could also be understood as "six wings per creature" or "around them," which relates to the spatial meaning.
G0303.origine: The Greek word "ana" originally expresses movement upward or backward, a notion of ascent or return. That is why it is found as a prefix in many verbs: "anabaïnein" (to ascend), "anagennân" (to be born again), "anakamptin" (to return). As a preposition or adverb of distribution, the meaning has specialized: the idea of "each one" comes from that of successive separation or distinction — each in their turn, each apart. This word is rare in New Testament Greek and much more common in classical Greek and 1st-century papyri.
G0303.emploi: "Ana" appears about 13 times in the New Testament, almost always in Matthew, Luke, Paul, and John. The most frequent context is that of distribution: in Matthew 20:9-10, regarding wages paid individually; in Luke 9:14, concerning groups that sit in rows; in Revelation 4:8, describing the number of wings each creature possesses. In 1 Corinthians 14:27, the word governs liturgical order — whoever speaks in tongues must do so each in turn. In Mark 7:31 and in other uses, it can also express spatial meaning or the idea of passage "through" or "among." The word primarily reflects the common Greek practice to indicate individual or successive distribution within a community or action.
G0303.portee: This word reminds the reader of an important truth: God cares about each individual, not just the crowd in general. When one sees "each" in the biblical text, it suggests that the Lord looks at each person, grants them their own value, and entrusts them with a distinct responsibility or gift. It is a comfort for those who feel lost in the mass: one is never anonymous before God.

sens: A step of a staircase, a step to ascend
A set of steps forming a staircase
By extension, a level of progression or a step to be taken
G0304.detail:
1. The word primarily designates an individual step of a staircase — a degree on which one places their foot to ascend. In Acts 21:35, Paul is on the "degrees" of the temple when the crowd mistreats him: this refers to a concrete staircase leading up to the Antonia fortress.
2. In the plural, it refers to a complete staircase, a series of steps. It is also in Acts 21:40 that Paul stands "on the degrees" to address the crowd from an elevated position — like a speaker on a podium.
3. Figuratively, the word can evoke a passage, a step to climb. The Psalms 120 to 134 in Hebrew bore the title "Song of Ascents" or "Psalms of Degrees": these may have been songs that pilgrims sang while ascending to Jerusalem, step by step.
G0304.origine: The Greek word comes from anabainô ("to ascend") and bathos ("depth, degree"). The basic image is that of a step that elevates the one who ascends it. It translates the Hebrew word ma'alah ("ascent," "step of a staircase"), which is also used for the steps of King Solomon's throne in 1 Kings 10:19-20. The formation of the word with the suffix -thmos indicates a concrete and physical notion.
G0304.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, exclusively in Acts 21:35 and 21:40, during the same event: the apostle Paul is held and presented to the crowd from a staircase of the Jerusalem temple. Both uses refer to the same physical staircase, but from two angles: first, Paul is carried by the soldiers (v. 35), then he stands there to speak (v. 40). The context is very concrete: it is a real situation, that of a staircase allowing ascent to the fortress. This word shows how Luke (the author of Acts) narrated the events with precision, including material details that make the scene vivid.
G0304.portee: This passage reminds us that even in moments of danger and hostility, God places His servants in situations where they can bear witness. Paul, held by the soldiers but allowed to speak, uses this unexpected moment to share his message. The degrees of the temple thus become a place of proclamation of Christ, transforming an ordinary staircase into a platform for the Gospel.

sens: To move upward, going from a lower place to a higher place
To leave a place, to depart (notably to come out of water or a basin)
To board a boat or ship
To go somewhere, to head toward a specific place
To appear, to emerge, to manifest (for things)
To rise in the mind, to come to thought (for thoughts)
G0305.detail:
1. It is the physical movement of ascending, going upward: Jesus ascends a mountain (Matthew 14:23), a seed rises from the ground and becomes a plant (Mark 4:32), apostles ascend together to Jerusalem (Luke 2:42).
2. The verb is used to exit or depart from a place: Jesus comes out of the water of the Jordan after His baptism (Matthew 3:16), Simon Peter boards the boat (John 21:11 uses the same verb, where the idea of departing takes precedence over the vertical direction).
3. It designates the action of boarding a ship or boat, to embark: after taking leave, the apostles board the ship (Acts 21:6).
4. More broadly, to go somewhere, to head there: the disciples ascend to Jerusalem with Jesus (Matthew 20:17), some ascend to the temple (Luke 18:10).
5. For things without will: smoke rises from the earth (Revelation 8:4), locusts come out of the abyss (Revelation 9:2), the Holy Spirit rises from the streets of the city to prayer (Acts 10:4).
6. For events or mental states: troubling thoughts rise in the hearts of the disciples (Luke 24:38), or "what the eye has not seen" rises to the heart of man in grace (1 Corinthians 2:9).
G0305.origine: The verb is composed of ἀνα ("upward, back") and βαίνω ("to go, to walk, to move"). The Hebrew word it most often translates is עָלָה (ʿalâ), which has exactly the same meaning: to go upward, to ascend. The root conveys the image of progressing, elevating, a fundamental movement in biblical geography where Jerusalem is on a mountain.
G0305.emploi: The verb appears 78 times in the New Testament, very frequently in Luke, John, and in Acts. It is first used in a concrete and physical sense: ascending a mountain (Matthew 14:23), ascending to Jerusalem (Matthew 20:17), boarding a boat (John 21:11). It takes on a metaphorical sense when speaking of things without bodies: smoke rises (Revelation 8:4), prayers rise to God (Acts 10:4). In John, "to ascend" becomes theological: Jesus "ascends" to heaven (John 6:62, Ephesians 4:10), translating the exaltation of the risen Christ. Finally, it describes what rises in the mind or heart, such as the troubling thoughts of the disciples (Luke 24:38).
G0305.portee: The verb "to ascend" invites the reader to recognize that Jesus does not remain at the level of the world, but ascends to the Father. This ascension manifests His victory and glory. For the believer, the verb also reminds us that prayer ascends to God, that it is not in vain: it crosses the distance and reaches the One who listens. It is a word of assurance and hope.

sens: To push back a decision or action in time
To defer the examination of a matter
G0306.detail:
1. To push back a decision or action in time: the word designates the act of rejecting something forward, that is, placing it further in time. In Acts 24:22, Governor Felix "postpones" Paul's judgment, not rendering his decision immediately.
2. To defer the examination of a matter: it specifically means to adjourn a trial or question while waiting for more favorable circumstances or additional information. Felix adjourns the hearing because he is waiting for Lysias, the Roman commander.
G0306.origine: The word comes from the root "ballô" which means "to throw," preceded by the prefix "ana" ("upward," "back"). The image is that of throwing something back, thus pushing it away from oneself — hence "to postpone." The middle form (reflexive) suggests that the one who postpones acts for themselves, to their advantage. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates Hebrew terms such as "avar" (to pass) and "ata" (to cover), in various contexts.
G0306.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 24:22, where Felix "postpones" Paul's judgment. It is a technical word of judicial language: it describes the adjournment of a matter. The use of the middle (reflexive) form indicates that Felix acts according to his personal will. The Greek Old Testament uses it to translate several Hebrew verbs in various contexts (Psalms, books of Kings).
G0306.portee: This passage shows the delays and hesitations of human power in the face of the Gospel. Felix dared not condemn Paul but did not want to release him either: he postponed his decision. For the reader, it is a reminder that earthly authorities procrastinate, while God acts according to His plans. It also invites patience: God will judge in His time.

sens: To haul, pull something up (a net, a boat)
To make something rise, to lead to a higher place
Figuratively: to extract, to bring out
G0307.detail:
1. The literal meaning of the word is to pull or haul something up: it is the action of the fisherman who brings his net filled with fish up to the shore (Matthew 13:48). The image comes from the concrete action of lifting or raising a heavy object, like pulling a sail or a rope upwards.
2. More broadly, the word means to make something rise or lead something from a low place to a higher one, hence the idea of progressing or elevating.
3. Figuratively, the word can evoke the idea of extracting or bringing something out of its place, as when one removes something from a location to bring it to light.
G0307.origine: The word is formed from the prefix ἀνα- (upwards, back) and βιβάζω (to make rise, to drive), which itself comes from βαίνω (to walk, to go). It is the causative form of ἀναβαίνω (to go up, to ascend): while ἀναβαίνω describes the action of going up oneself, ἀναβιβάζω describes the action of making something else go up, usually with effort. In Hebrew, this verb often translates עָלָה in the causative form (to make rise), which denotes the action of elevating or hauling.
G0307.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 13:48, in the parable of the net thrown into the sea. Jesus describes the fishermen who pull their net filled with fish to the shore. The context is one of fruitful fishing: the net, full of fish, must be raised and hoisted with effort. The word concretely illustrates the work of the fishermen and prepares the spiritual lesson of the parable, where the Kingdom of Heaven is compared to a net that gathers the good and the bad, which must be sorted.
G0307.portee: This image of the net being drawn up, filled with an abundant harvest, evokes for the believer the idea of the harvest and the separation of the good and the bad on the day of judgment. It also reminds that God's work requires effort, a voluntary and persevering action, like that of the fisherman who pulls his net. The word invites us to see in the simple gestures of daily work an image of divine providence and the final gathering of the elect.

G0308.fr: to see or lift the eyes
sens: To turn one's gaze upwards or in a direction
To regain sight, to recover the ability to see
To look attentively, to observe something or someone
G0308.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to raise closed or lowered eyes to look upwards. In Luke 21:1, Jesus "lifted up his eyes" and observed the rich making their offerings. It is a simple gesture but rich in meaning: one no longer looks down, but focuses attention on something important.

2. To regain sight: to recover the ability to see after blindness. This is the dominant meaning among the evangelists. The blind man in Mark 10:51 asks Jesus to "regain sight," and after healing in Luke 18:42-43, he "saw" and followed Jesus, glorifying God. It is both a physical miracle and a spiritual sign of salvation.

3. To observe, to look intently at someone or something. In Mark 6:41, when Jesus breaks the bread, he "lifted his eyes to heaven," a gesture of prayer and gratitude. The gaze is not passive: it expresses a relationship, an intention.
G0308.origine: The word combines "ana" (upwards, back) and "blepo" (to see, to look). It literally means "to look upwards or back." The root "blepo" is common in classical Greek for verbs of vision. The underlying Hebrew word in the Old Testament is often "nasa" (to lift, to elevate), which emphasizes the link between the physical action of lifting and that of looking or seeing.
G0308.emploi: The verb appears 23 times in the New Testament, mostly among the evangelists (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and in Acts. It is divided into two major uses: 1) To lift or raise the eyes (Mark 6:41, 7:34, Luke 9:16, 21:1, John 4:35), a gesture of prayer, blessing, or spiritual attention. 2) To regain sight, the dominant sense in the miracles of Jesus (Matthew 11:5, Mark 10:51-52, Luke 7:22, 18:42-43, John 9:11, 9:15, Acts 9:12, 9:17-18, 22:13). In this second case, the verb embodies a messianic sign: Jesus restores sight to the blind, fulfilling the promise of Isaiah. Each account emphasizes the power of Jesus and the faith of the healed.
G0308.portee: Regaining sight is much more than a physical miracle: it is an image of the transformation that Jesus brings. The healed blind man in John 9 becomes a witness to the light of Christ. For the Christian reader, this word invites us to ask Jesus to heal our spiritual blindness, our prejudices, and our misunderstandings, so that we may truly see and follow him. Lifting our eyes to heaven is to adopt a posture of worship and gratitude towards God.

sens: The action of regaining sight, the ability to see after being blind
Spiritual restoration of perception and divine understanding
G0309.detail:
1. The word literally designates the moment when someone who was blind regains the ability to see. It is the instant when light becomes visible, when the eyes open again to the world. In Luke 4:18, Jesus announces that his ministry brings recovery of sight to the blind, among other deliverances and restorations.
2. Figuratively, regaining sight symbolizes spiritual and moral healing: regaining the right vision of God and His will, seeing clearly after being in the darkness of ignorance or error. It is to regain spiritual understanding, the lost discernment.
G0309.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and is composed of two parts: the prefix "ana" (return, recommencement) and the verb "blepo" (to see, to look). The starting image is that of the gaze rising, straightening, coming back to life. The related verb "anablepein" (to look upwards, to see again) is used to describe the action of regaining sight. This expression translates in Greek the Hebrew of the Old Testament that speaks of the opening of the eyes of the blind, a central motif of the salvation brought by the Messiah.
G0309.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:18, where Jesus reads the passage from Isaiah 61:1 declaring: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor; he has sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind." It is a programmatic passage: Jesus lists the signs of his messianic ministry. Regaining sight figures as one of the great restorations that his coming brings, symbolizing both physical healings and the spiritual transformation of those who receive him.
G0309.portee: For the disciple, this word reminds us that Christ came not only to heal physical ailments but also and especially to open the eyes of the soul. It invites us to recognize Jesus as the Messiah spoken of by the prophets, the one who truly liberates. It is also a call: have we regained spiritual sight in encountering him, or do we still live in darkness?

sens: Cry out, let out a powerful cry
Express one's anguish or distress with a heartfelt cry
G0310.detail:
1. The verb denotes the action of crying out loud with force and intensity. It is a cry that resonates, that can be heard from afar. In Matthew 27:46, Jesus on the cross lets out a cry: "Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?'" — it is the very cry of his soul in ultimate suffering.
2. Beyond mere noise, the word expresses a cry laden with feeling, a word torn from the being by intense emotion or distress. It is not speaking calmly: it is letting out what one cannot hold back.
G0310.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "ana-" (upward, outward) and "boaō" (to cry, to call). This composition suggests a cry that rises, that elevates. In Hebrew, the Old Testament used several verbs from the same semantic field — "tzaaq," "zaaaq," "qarah" — all rendered by equivalent Greek words to express the cry of the heart that addresses God or bursts forth in distress.
G0310.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament. It is Matthew who chooses it to report Jesus' cry on the cross, a moment of abandonment and extreme suffering where the Son addresses God with his heart-wrenching question. This unique cry in the gospel underscores the intensity and authenticity of Jesus' human pain in the face of divine silence.
G0310.portee: This word invites us to recognize that prayer is not always a whisper or tranquil wisdom: it can be a cry, urgency, distress that speaks to God directly. Jesus himself cried out. This allows the believer to bring before God not only polished words but also heartfelt cries, unanswered questions, and true suffering.

sens: Postpone, let time pass before acting
Not do immediately what is requested
G0311.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of postponing a decision or action to a later time. In Acts 25:17, Governor Festus explains that he did not delay in examining Paul's case: he sat down immediately on his tribunal and promptly ordered the accused to be brought in. The term thus evokes hesitation, delay, or even a refusal to act.
2. More broadly, it is the attitude of one who shrinks from a responsibility or obligation. To refuse to delay means to act promptly, without dragging things out.
G0311.origine: The Greek word ἀναβολή comes from the verb ἀναβάλλω (anaballo), composed of ἀνά (ana, "up, again") and βάλλω (ballô, "to throw"). The original image is that of "pushing up or aside," hence "to differ, to postpone." This root carries the idea of a delay, of putting something on hold.
G0311.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 25:17. The context is judicial: Festus, the Roman governor of Judea, justifies his conduct by explaining that he did not make the mistake of delaying his judgment on Paul's case. On the contrary, he acted without delay, thus demonstrating his respect for the procedure and his administrative efficiency. The use of the word reveals the stakes of Roman justice: agreeing to delay could seem suspicious or ineffective.
G0311.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of swift action in the face of responsibilities that fall upon us, particularly in matters of justice and truth. For the Christian, it invites us not to postpone decisions that require courage or commitment, and to recognize that delaying can be a form of cowardice or neglect of duty.

sens: Report news, make known what one has learned
Proclaim, publicly declare a message or truth
Communicate a received word to convey
G0312.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to report news, to make known something that one has learned or witnessed. It is to carry information from one place or person to another. In Acts 15:4, the disciples "reported all that God had done with them" — they were sharing the account of their missionary experiences.
2. The word then takes on a broader meaning: to announce or publicly declare a truth, a teaching, a word intended to be heard. In John 4:25, the Samaritan woman says of the Messiah: "When he comes, he will announce to us all things" — he will reveal and proclaim the mysteries of God.
3. More specifically, the word denotes the action of communicating a word that comes from elsewhere and that one transmits faithfully. In John 16:13-15, the Spirit of truth "will announce to you the things to come" — he will have no other function than to convey what he has received from the Father, without adding anything of his own.
G0312.origine: The Greek word ἀναγγέλλω (anangellō) is composed of the prefix ἀνά- (aná: "up, back") and the verb ἀγγέλλω (angéllō: "to announce, to report"). It expresses the idea of reporting a message by bringing it back to someone, or proclaiming it upward. The root ἀγγέλλω is related to the noun ἄγγελος (angélos: "messenger, angel"), the one who carries and delivers a word. In Hebrew, this verb often translates נָגַד (nagad: "to make known, to report"), which has the same meaning of disclosure and revelation.
G0312.emploi: The verb appears 14 times in the New Testament, mainly in John and in Acts. It denotes the act of reporting news (Acts 15:4: "they reported") or announcing a teaching (John 4:25, 16:13). In the Gospel of John, it particularly characterizes the work of the Holy Spirit, who announces things to come by transmitting the Father's word (16:13-15). In Paul, in Romans 15:21, it refers to the proclamation of the Gospel to those who have not heard it. The word always emphasizes the act of carrying a received word and communicating it to others, with the idea of faithfulness to what has been entrusted.
G0312.portee: This word reminds Christians that the announcement of the Gospel and the transmission of God's word are not human inventions, but the faithful communication of a received message. Just as the Holy Spirit announces what he has heard from the Father, the disciple who announces the Good News participates in this same work of transmission. It is a responsibility: one adds nothing of oneself, but reports and proclaims what has been entrusted to us.

sens: To beget again, to give a new birth
To be spiritually reborn through the action of God
To be transformed internally by divine power
G0313.detail: 1. The word literally means "to give birth again": it is the action of giving birth a second time. In the Bible, it never refers to a physical birth, but to a profound spiritual transformation. 2. Regeneration is the work of God that gives us new life through His Spirit. In 1 Peter 1:3, the believer is "born again to a living hope" — God enables us to hope in the resurrection, just as He raised Jesus. 3. This new birth occurs "not of corruptible seed, but of the living and enduring word of God" (1 Peter 1:23): it is not physical heritage that saves us, but the Gospel that produces in us a new and indestructible life.
G0313.origine: The word combines the prefix "ana-" (which means "again, back") with "gennaō" ("to beget, to give birth"). It literally means "to give birth again". The root "gennao" appears throughout the New Testament to speak of procreation or, in a spiritual sense, a new birth given by God. The concept aligns with that of "new birth" in Greek "paliggenesia" (general regeneration) or "gennēthē anōthen" (to be born from above), found in John.
G0313.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the first epistle of Peter (1:3 and 1:23), where it describes the action of God making us spiritually reborn. Peter uses this term to assure the scattered and persecuted Christians that they have received a new and indestructible life, based not on human transmission (the flesh), but on the eternal word of God. In 1 Peter 1:3, regeneration creates in us the living hope of resurrection; in 1 Peter 1:23, it emphasizes that this new life comes from the incorruptible seed of the Gospel, not from our fleshly lineage.
G0313.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the evangelical message: none of us is condemned by our birth or earthly origins. God offers every believer a new birth, a radically different beginning, which frees him from sin and fills him with a living hope. Regeneration is not a human effort, but an action of the living word of God — it is as certain and effective as the resurrection of Jesus.

sens: To recognize, to identify something one already knows
To read written characters, to decipher a text
To read aloud, to make a reading in front of others
To understand the meaning of what one reads
G0314.detail:
1. The primary meaning is "to recognize", that is, to identify something one has already encountered or should know. This is why we find this word in questions like "Have you not read?" (Matthew 12:3, Mark 12:10), where "to read" means "have you read and thus known, recognized this story".
2. The main sense, which appears throughout the New Testament, is "to read" in the sense of deciphering written characters: Jesus tells the young man "Read in the Scriptures" (Matthew 21:42), the Ethiopian eunuch "was reading" the prophet Isaiah as he scanned it (Acts 8:30).
3. Very often, reading is done aloud, especially in the synagogue or before an assembly: "He stood up to read", it is said of Jesus in Nazareth (Luke 4:16), and the letters of the Apostle Paul were to be "read" before the churches (1 Thessalonians 5:27, Colossians 4:16).
4. Reading also implies understanding: when the eunuch asks Philip, "Do you understand what you are reading?" (Acts 8:30), the two ideas go together — to read is to receive the written message.
G0314.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: "ana" (again) and "ginōskō" (to know). The image is that of "to know again", that is, to recognize what was known. By reading characters, one recognizes them, identifies them. The root "ginōskō" means "to know" and appears in other important Greek words. This verb often translates the Hebrew word "qara", which means both "to cry out" and "to read aloud" — showing that in the Bible, reading was normally to be heard.
G0314.emploi: This verb appears about 30 times in the New Testament, concentrated mostly in the Gospels and the letters of Paul. It is almost always used to speak of the reading of the Scriptures: the Pharisees question Jesus by citing what they "have not read", Jesus Himself cites "written" passages that should be "read", the Ethiopian eunuch "reads" the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. Reading often takes place before witnesses (which is why Paul's letters must be "read" in church), and it already implied understanding, as shown by Philip's question. The context is almost always religious: the Law, the Prophets, the apostolic letters are read.
G0314.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible is not a magical text that one simply possesses by holding it: we must read it, that is, study it, recognize it, understand it. Reading the Scriptures is to come into contact with the word of God. When Jesus asks, "Have you not read?", He calls His listeners to truly know the Scripture, not just to have heard it. The model of the eunuch reading Isaiah with Philip's help shows that reading Scripture can lead to faith when one receives the explanation and understands it.

sens: To force someone to do something by strength or by irresistible pressure
To force someone to act against their will or natural inclination
To impose an absolute necessity, leaving no choice
G0315.detail: 1. The word describes the action of forcing someone to perform an act: it is a constraint exercised by force or by an authority that leaves no escape. Jesus "compelled" His disciples to get into the boat (Matthew 14:22, Mark 6:45): it was a clear and imperative instruction, not a mere suggestion. 2. The word also applies to psychological or moral pressure that removes the freedom to act otherwise. Paul reports that he was "compelled" to commend himself to the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 12:11): it was not his intention, but circumstances forced him to do so. 3. In the account of the servant inviting the poor to the feast, the master says: "those you find, compel them to enter" (Luke 14:23), suggesting an insistence that does not tolerate refusal. 4. The word can also describe violent or oppressive constraint: Paul confesses to having "compelled" Christians to blaspheme during his persecutions (Acts 26:11), showing here the brutality of coercion.
G0315.origine: The word comes from the root ἀνάγκη ("necessity, constraint"), which evokes an inevitable force, something one cannot escape. This root also appears in the French word "angoisse". The verb adds the idea of an action: the one who compels imposes this necessity on someone else. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew שֹׁטֵר ("commander, one who orders"), confirming its link with authority and obligation.
G0315.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and the letters of Paul. In Matthew and Mark, Jesus "compels" His disciples to perform a task (to get into the boat). Luke uses it to express the pressing invitation of the master of the feast. Paul uses it to describe his own actions: he confesses to having "compelled" Christians to blaspheme (Acts 26:11), and he recounts his circumstances where he was "compelled" to appeal to Caesar (Acts 28:19). In Galatians, the verb appears regarding the issue of circumcision and observances, showing how false teachers attempted to "compel" obedience to the Law. The word always retains the idea of pressure or force that removes free choice.
G0315.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the difference between legitimate authority that commands for the good of others (like Jesus) and oppressive or tyrannical constraint (like that which Paul once exercised against Christians). It also shows how true disciples obey not out of terror, but out of trust in the one who commands. For the Christian, it is a call to examine whether he obeys freely to Jesus Christ or if he resists out of fear of being "compelled."

sens: That which is indispensable, that cannot be avoided or ignored
That which is imposed by the force of circumstances, which does not allow for delay
That which is important, useful, that must be done or accomplished
That which is close, intimate, bound by strong ties
G0316.detail:
1. What is necessary is what must absolutely be had or done: one cannot do without it. Thus, in 1 Corinthians 12:22, the members of the body that seem the weakest are "necessary" — the body could not function without them. This conveys the idea of indispensability.
2. The word can also express a necessity that arises from a situation, which imposes itself. In Acts 13:46, it was "necessary" that the word of God be announced first to the Jews — it was the established order, what was to happen naturally.
3. Sometimes, it is translated as "duty" or "obligation": it is a moral or practical necessity, something deemed indispensable to do. Paul considers it "necessary" to send Epaphroditus to the Philippians (Philippians 2:25), meaning he must do it, it is important.
4. The word can also qualify a personal relationship: the "intimate friends" (Acts 10:24) are those who are close, bound by a close and necessary friendship. This conveys a sense of intimacy, an essential closeness.
G0316.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "anagké," which means "constraint" or "necessity." This root evokes the idea of force, of what presses and constrains. The adjective "necessary" describes what is imposed by this force, what cannot be otherwise. This family of words appears several times in the New Testament to express obligation or the inevitable.
G0316.emploi: The word appears eight times in the New Testament, always in Paul or in later letters (Acts, Paul's epistles, Hebrews). It primarily denotes what is indispensable: the weak members of the body, the resources for living (Philippians 1:24), the collection to be prepared (2 Corinthians 9:5). It also expresses a necessity of order or obligation: the announcement of the Gospel to the Jews first (Acts 13:46), the sending of a brother (Philippians 2:25), the fulfillment of good works (Titus 3:14). Only once does it qualify a personal relationship: the "intimate friends" of Cornelius (Acts 10:24). The meaning thus nuances between the indispensable objective and the practical or moral obligation.
G0316.portee: This word invites the Christian to distinguish the essential from the accessory. By emphasizing what is "necessary," Scripture calls us to wisdom: to know what cannot be lacking (the weak members of the body of Christ, faith, love), and also to obedience — to recognize when God makes something "necessary" in our lives. It is a call to clarity of vision and faithfulness in what truly matters.

sens: under the effect of an external force
against one's will
by obligation rather than by choice
without inner freedom
G0317.detail: 1. The word describes an action done under the pressure of an external force, against the natural desire of the one performing it — like doing something because one is forced to. 2. It is the exact opposite of free and voluntary choice: to act by constraint means to obey an imposed necessity rather than to follow one's own inclination. 3. In 1 Peter 5:2, Peter exhorts the elders to shepherd the flock of God "not by constraint, but willingly": he distinguishes between two motivations for pastoral action, one external and coercive, the other internal and freely consented.
G0317.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "necessity, constraint" (the same root as in the French word "angoisse"). The adverb derives from the noun designating what is inevitable or forced. It is the direct opposite of the Greek word ἑκουσίως, "willingly, of one's own accord," which appears in the same verse.
G0317.emploi: This word is very rare in the New Testament: it occurs only once in 1 Peter 5:2. Peter uses it to remind the elders that their pastoral mission should never be a burden imposed from the outside, but a service motivated by love for Christ and the flock. The adverb emphasizes the crucial difference between forced obedience and freely chosen devotion — a central theme of Christian ethics.
G0317.portee: This word sheds light on an essential truth: authentic Christian service does not arise from external constraint, but from the transformation of the heart. For a pastor, a leader, or any committed believer, it serves as a reminder that if one acts only out of obligation or under pressure, one has lost the spirit of service. Love freely given is the only force capable of nurturing a sustainable and fruitful ministry.

sens: that which cannot not be, that which imposes itself inevitably
the obligation, the constraint that weighs on someone
distress, calamity, difficult trial
G0318.detail:
1. The primary meaning is logical or inevitable necessity: that which must happen without being avoidable. When Jesus says "it is necessary that scandals come" (Matthew 18:7), he asserts that these things must occur in the order of things — not as a curse, but as an unavoidable reality. Similarly, "it is necessary for the death of the testator to be established" (Hebrews 9:16) for a will to be valid: it is a condition that imposes itself.
2. The word then designates the obligation or constraint that is exerted on a person. Paul writes: "a necessity is laid upon me" (1 Corinthians 9:16) — he feels the weight of a mission he cannot refuse, as if an external force is pressing him. It conveys the idea of something that binds your hands, forcing you to act against your will. Philemon 1:14 contrasts the "forced" gift (under constraint) with the voluntary and free gift.
3. In a third sense, anagkē designates distress, calamity, trial. Luke speaks of pregnant women in "distress" (21:23) — not merely an abstract obligation, but the concrete suffering they endure. The difficulties Paul enumerates (2 Corinthians 6:4 and 12:10) are the "calamities" that press him on all sides, the hard knocks of life.
G0318.origine: The Greek word anagkē comes from a root that evokes narrowness, strangulation, compression: something that tightens around you, that traps you. The family of the word includes anagkázō ("to constrain," "to force"), where the sense of constraining force is explicit. In the Septuagint, ancient Greek often translates Hebrew words designating distress and compression (צַר tsár, "narrow," "adversary"), confirming the basic image: a necessity is what presses you, crushes you, leaves you with no escape.
G0318.emploi: The word appears about 18 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul and in the epistle to the Hebrews. It is first used to express the inevitable logical or theological necessity: it is necessary for such an event to happen (Matthew 18:7, Hebrews 9:16, 9:23). It then describes the constraint experienced by a person: being obliged to do something against one's will (Luke 23:17: Pilate was compelled to release a prisoner at the feast). Paul makes it the key term of his apostolic experience: he feels an urgent necessity that drives him to preach, regardless of his personal will. Finally, the word designates trials and tribulations: the "calamities" (1 Corinthians 7:26, 2 Corinthians 6:4) that believers go through. Depending on the context, anagkē oscillates between the abstract (what must be) and the concrete (what presses, what suffers).
G0318.portee: For the Christian, this word illuminates the tension between freedom and divine order. God never constrains by brute force, but His purposes are accomplished with a necessity that no one can prevent. Paul also shows that God's call, while free, imposes itself on the one who hears it with an irresistible force: it is a necessity that is not crushing, but liberating. Finally, the word reminds us that the trials of Christians are not accidents, but part of the reality of the world; enduring them with joy and obedience is to enter into a higher logic that alone gives meaning to suffering.

sens: Identify someone who was not initially distinguished or who was forgotten
G0319.detail: 1. To recognize means here to identify and clearly distinguish someone after not having known them or after a separation. In Acts 7:13, Joseph is finally recognized by his brothers during their second encounter in Egypt: after years of separation and not having seen him grow into the role of governor, they discover his true identity. The word evokes that moment when the veil falls and one says, 'Ah, it's you!'.
G0319.origine: The Greek word ἀναγνωρίζω (anagnōrizō) is composed of the prefix ἀνα- (ana-, 'again') and the verb γνωρίζω (gnōrizō, 'to make known, to recognize'), which derives from γνῶσις (gnôsis, 'knowledge'). The starting image is that of returning to the knowledge of someone. In biblical Hebrew, the same meaning is conveyed by יָדַע (yada, 'to know'), which denotes concrete knowledge and recognizing someone.
G0319.emploi: This verb appears only once in the preserved New Testament (Acts 7:13), in Stephen's speech recounting the story of Joseph. Stephen tells how, during his brothers' second visit to Egypt, Joseph made himself known to them — the moment when his hidden identity is finally revealed. This context emphasizes the biblical theme of recognition and the revelation of one who was thought to be lost or misunderstood.
G0319.portee: This word reminds the reader of a powerful theme: sometimes, we encounter someone or something without truly recognizing it. Joseph, the exalted governor, is recognized only when he reveals himself. This invites reflection on the revelation of God and His work: often, we only recognize His hand when He clearly manifests Himself.

sens: Action of reading aloud before an assembly
Action of reading a written text
Recognition, identification of something
G0320.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word in the New Testament is that of public reading, particularly of the Holy Scriptures in the synagogue. In Acts 13:15, after the reading of the Law and the Prophets during the synagogue service, the leaders invite someone to speak — this is a communal and official act.
2. By extension, the word denotes the action of reading in general, the act of going through a text. In 1 Timothy 4:13, Paul exhorts Timothy to devote himself to reading — not only to read for himself, but to meditate and study the Scriptures.
3. In a broader sense, ἀνάγνωσις can mean the recognition or identification of something, as shown by its etymology — seeing a text and recognizing it. In 2 Corinthians 3:14, the veil that covers the Old Testament prevents the Jews from truly recognizing it, that is, from seeing in it the fulfillment in Christ.
G0320.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ἀνα- ('again', 'up') and γνῶσις ('knowledge', from γι-γνώ-σκω 'to know'). The starting image is that of recognizing again or knowing from a reading: seeing something written and distinguishing it, identifying it. The family of the word includes ἀναγιγνώσκω ('to read') and γνῶσις ('knowledge'). In the Greek of the Septuagint, it translates the Hebrew מִקְרָא (miqrá, 'that which is called, proclaimed'), which also denotes the public reading of the Law.
G0320.emploi: The word appears 3 times in the New Testament, always in the context of reading Scripture. In Acts 13:15, it is the official synagogue reading of the Law and the Prophets. In 1 Timothy 4:13, Paul recommends that Timothy devote time to reading with exhortation and teaching — a pastoral ministry that relies on a deep knowledge of the Word. In 2 Corinthians 3:14, Paul speaks of the veil that remains 'when they read' the Old Testament: the word takes on an existential hue, as it is the reading of the text that is blurred by the refusal to recognize Christ. Each time, reading is not a silent and solitary activity, but an act that engages understanding and sometimes the community.
G0320.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the central importance of reading the Word of God in the life of faith. It is not an end in itself: it should lead to the recognition of Christ throughout Scripture and to the teaching of the people. For the servant of God, like Timothy, diligent reading of the Word is a primary duty. And for every believer, this word invites us not to read Scripture superficially, but with a heart willing to recognize the person and work of Jesus Christ.

sens: To lead someone from one place to another
To take someone with you on a journey or trip
To lead to a specific place or goal
To set sail, to leave port by boat
To present or offer something (in a liturgical sense)
G0321.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to lead or guide: to take someone from one place to another. Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness (Matthew 4:1), and Peter is taken to the upper room where the deceased Dorcas is (Acts 9:39).
2. The word is used for intentional movement: one departs with others, taking them along. Paul and his companions embark at Paphos to go to Pamphylia (Acts 13:13).
3. It can indicate going toward a goal or a defined place: departing from Ephesus means leaving that city in the direction of elsewhere (Acts 18:21).
4. In the middle voice (in a nautical sense), the verb means 'to set sail' or 'to take to the sea': the disciples get into a boat and depart to cross the lake (Luke 8:22). This is the sense often found in Acts when speaking of boat journeys.
5. In a sacrificial context, the verb can mean 'to offer' or 'to present': to offer a sacrifice to God (Acts 7:41).
G0321.origine: The word is composed of ἀνά ('upward, backward, back') and ἄγω ('to lead, to bring'). It evokes the idea of leading someone backward or upward — hence 'to depart' or 'to go away'. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it generally translates עָלָה ('to ascend'), hence the image of setting out. The word belongs to the family of ἄγω, from which ἀγωγή ('conduct, way of life') also derives.
G0321.emploi: The verb appears 23 times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts (18 occurrences). In the senses of 'to lead' or 'to take', it describes terrestrial movements: Jesus is led into the wilderness (Matthew 4:1), Peter is taken to Dorcas (Acts 9:39). But the dominant usage is nautical: 'to depart, to embark, to set sail'. The journeys of Paul and his companions by boat to Judea, Macedonia, or Malta provide the most numerous examples (Luke 8:22; Acts 13:13, 16:11, 20:3, 21:1, 27:2). Romans 10:7 and Hebrews 13:20 use it in the figurative sense of 'bringing out of' (the dead).
G0321.portee: This verb reminds us that the steps of the disciples — and ours — are guided by God or submitted to His will. Jesus is led by the Spirit, not of His own accord (Matthew 4:1). The journeys of Paul in Acts also show that God directs the path of those who serve Him, even through storms and perils at sea. The word invites the Christian to trust in divine direction, even when the road is uncertain.

sens: Publicly show, manifest
Choose and appoint someone for a position
G0322.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to openly show, to make known publicly: it is to bring something or someone to light, to 'lift' it to make it visible to all. In Acts 1:24, the disciples pray to God to show, to designate which of the two candidates He has chosen to replace Judas — it is about revealing God's choice.
2. From this comes the meaning of choosing and establishing someone in a role or mission. It is to publicly install a person in their function. In Luke 10:1, the Lord 'designates' seventy disciples and sends them on a mission: He chooses and establishes them for this work.
G0322.origine: The word is composed of ana ('upward') and deiknumi ('to show'). The basic image is therefore one of lifting and exhibiting, making visible by elevating. This composition reflects a concrete movement — lifting something to make it apparent — that the Bible transposes to the action of designating a person, placing them in prominence for a role.
G0322.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, according to the provided usages. In Acts 1:24, it is about the apostles asking God to reveal His choice between two men. In Luke 10:1, Jesus actively 'designates' seventy disciples for a mission. In both cases, the verb combines the idea of manifesting and establishing: one does not designate in secret; one designates to publicly show who has been chosen and why. It is a decisive and visible act.
G0322.portee: This verb teaches us that God chooses His workers and does so clearly and publicly, not arbitrarily. When Jesus designates the seventy, He manifests His authority and intention to continue His work through sent ones. For the believer, this means that our calling, our place in the body of Christ, is not due to chance: God designates us, shows us, and establishes us in a mission, and it is up to us to respond to this visible call.

sens: Official manifestation of a person before the people
Solemn revelation or announcement of someone
Action of showing, publicly exhibiting
G0323.detail:
1. The word refers to the official appearance of a person in public, the moment when they show themselves or are shown to the eyes of all. Luke uses it for John the Baptist: 'he remained in the deserts until the day he presented himself before Israel' (Luke 1:80), meaning the moment when John left the desert to publicly manifest himself to Israel and begin his ministry.
2. More broadly, the word evokes an announcement or revelation: not an accidental appearance, but an intentional, official presentation meant to make someone known. This is why the translation 'presentation' fits better than simply 'appearance.'
3. The underlying image is one of showing, exhibiting, bringing to light: something or someone that was hidden becomes visible and recognizable.
G0323.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀναδείκνυμι (anadeíknumi), formed from ἀνά (aná, 'upward, forward') and δείκνυμι (deíknumi, 'to show'). The idea is to 'show forward,' to reveal or manifest. The preposition ἀνά adds a notion of solemnity or fullness: it is not a simple manifestation, but a complete and official presentation. Related words expressing actions of showing or revealing are found elsewhere in the New Testament.
G0323.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:80, to describe the moment when John the Baptist left the desert and publicly presented himself to Israel. Luke uses it to mark a decisive turning point: after years of retreat and spiritual preparation, John enters the official scene to fulfill his mission. This term emphasizes the solemn and anticipated nature of this manifestation, as if it were the culmination of a period of hidden maturation.
G0323.portee: This word reminds the reader that the life of faith often involves hidden preparation before a public manifestation. John the Baptist was spiritually strengthened in the desert before becoming the forerunner of the Messiah. For the believer, this means that the time of silent preparation and rooting in God is never wasted: it leads to a time when God entrusts us with a visible task, a presentation of ourselves in service.

sens: Welcome someone, give them hospitality
Accept, take on oneself a responsibility or a promise
G0324.detail:
1. To receive someone as a host, to offer them hospitality and lodging. It is the warm welcome of a traveler: in Malta, Publius 'received' Paul and his companions, lodging them for three days 'in the most friendly manner' (Acts 28:7). The verb evokes both the opening of the heart and the welcoming of the body.
2. To accept, take upon oneself a responsibility or a promised good. Abraham 'received' God's promises — not just once, but he carried them within him, bearing them as a living burden throughout his life of faith. When he offered Isaac, he acted as one who 'had received' these promises and held them to be true (Hebrews 11:17).
G0324.origine: The word is composed of 'ana-' (up, again) and 'dechomai' (to receive, to welcome). The basic image is that of taking or receiving something into one's hands, with a movement towards oneself. The verb often translates the Hebrew לָקַח (laqaḥ, to take) and expresses the idea of an active, conscious taking — one does not receive passively, but welcomes, assumes what is given to us.
G0324.emploi: The verb appears twice in the preserved New Testament. In Acts 28:7, it refers to concrete hospitality: Publius 'receives' the shipwrecked with kindness. In Hebrews 11:17, it takes on a more spiritual and abstract meaning: Abraham 'received' the divine promises, which means he was their living bearer, the one who carried them in his heart and guided his faith. The word can thus shift from the concrete (welcoming a guest) to the abstract (accepting and keeping a promise).
G0324.portee: This verb teaches us two things about faith. First, Christian hospitality is not a detail: it is a form of conscious and generous reception. Second, 'receiving' God's promises does not mean a completed past event, but a living, ongoing welcome — this is how Abraham, years after the promise, still 'held' it, to the point of being ready to offer it to God.

sens: Hand over, entrust something or someone to someone else
Transmit a message or an official document
G0325.detail:
1. The word expresses the action of giving or entrusting something (a letter, a person) to another person, passing it from one hand to another. It is the concrete gesture of rendering or transferring the responsibility of what one carries. In Acts 23:33, the Roman horsemen 'deliver' the letter to the governor: they no longer keep it, they transfer it to the one who needs to know about it.
2. In this official context, the word emphasizes the formal transmission of a document or a person in a chain of command. The soldiers fulfill their mission: they have received the order to escort Paul and the letter from Lysias to Felix, and they now 'deliver' them to the final recipient.
G0325.origine: The word combines the prefix *ana* ('upward, again') and the verb *didōmi* ('to give'). The starting image is that of 'giving back' or 'delivering,' particularly in passing something from low to high or from one person to another. In ancient Greek, this verb is also used in the sense of 'producing, making grow' (a plant that 'sends' its stems upward), but in Acts it takes on the meaning of 'deliver, entrust.'
G0325.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 23:33. In this historical passage, Lysias's horsemen urgently escort Paul and a letter to Felix, the Roman governor. When they arrive in Caesarea, they 'deliver' the prisoner and the document to the governor. The context is one of military and administrative procedure: each officer must account for and transfer their load to the next superior.
G0325.portee: This word shows how a simple action — delivering a letter — fits into a plan that God controls. Paul, a prisoner, is transported and entrusted from hand to hand, but it is the Lord who directs the events. For the reader, it is a lesson in trust: even in official procedures and the hands of authorities, God remains in control of what happens.

sens: To return to physical life, to regain life after death or a near-death experience
To regain strength and vigor, to return to activity
To be morally or spiritually reborn
To reappear, to manifest again
G0326.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to come back to life, to regain existence after having been dead or dying. It is life that is reborn in someone. In the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:24), the father says of his son, "was dead, and is alive again": the young man, lost far from home, is found and returns; this physical resurrection of the journey is also an image of his spiritual return to life.
2. The word is also used in a moral and spiritual sense: it is an inner awakening, a rebirth of what was dead within us. In Romans 7:9, Paul says that "sin revived": the commandment of God brings to life the sin that was dormant in him, awakens it, and makes it active in his conscience. It is the new life that emerges where moral or spiritual death once reigned.
G0326.origine: The word comes from the prefix "ana-" (again, back) and "zaō" (to live). It literally means "to live again." The root "zaō" (to live) is one of the most fundamental in Greek: it appears in words like "zōē" (life, vital principle) and "zoion" (animal, living creature). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this Greek verb often translates "chayah" (to live, to exist), especially when it comes to returning to life or continuing to live.
G0326.emploi: This verb appears twice in the New Testament, in two very different contexts that show the richness of its meaning. In Luke 15:24, in the parable of the prodigal son, it describes the return to life of the young man who was lost: it is a resurrection that is both concrete (he returns) and spiritual (he returns to his father). In Romans 7:9, Paul uses it paradoxically: sin "revives" when the commandment comes, meaning that the divine law awakens and revives the dormant conscience of sin. These two uses show that the word always denotes a return to life, a resurrection or awakening, whether physical, moral, or spiritual.
G0326.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the Christian: it reminds us that conversion is a true resurrection, a return to life after having been dead in sin. For one who turns away from God, it is a spiritual death; returning to God is to come back to life, to be reborn. It is also a call to vigilance: sin never truly dies within us; it can be reborn if we let our spiritual guard down. Finally, this term elevates the heart: only God gives true life, and it is to Him that we owe our resurrection, which begins here and will be completed in eternity.

sens: To search for someone or something by rummaging, exploring
To look for someone attentively when one does not know where to find them
To inquire, to ask about someone's presence or whereabouts
G0327.detail:
1. The word describes the action of searching in detail, exploring places or asking questions: Mary and Joseph "sought" Jesus among their traveling companions, then "sought him" again in Jerusalem (Luke 2:44-45), which implies a real difficulty; they truly did not know where he was.
2. To seek a particular person, especially when they have disappeared or when one does not know where they are: this is what Barnabas did when he "sought" Saul in Tarsus (Acts 11:25), meaning he inquired about his whereabouts and actively searched for him.
3. This search can also include the idea of inquiring, asking others to find someone.
G0327.origine: The word is formed from the prefix ἀνα- ("up," "again," "in detail") and ζητέω ("to seek"). It suggests a search that goes up, explores, or restarts — hence the idea of an active and meticulous search. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament uses similar words like דָּרַשׁ (darash, "to seek," "to inquire") or בָּקַשׁ (baqash, "to seek").
G0327.emploi: This verb appears 3 times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Gospels and Acts. It always describes a difficult or urgent human search. Luke uses it twice to recount how Joseph and Mary sought Jesus in Jerusalem after not finding him on the road (Luke 2:44-45): this is the only time the young Jesus voluntarily disappears before his passion. Acts uses it to describe how Barnabas had to seek Saul in Tarsus before bringing him to Antioch (Acts 11:25), a decisive moment in the birth of the international church. In both cases, the search is successful: the child Jesus is found in the Temple, and Saul is brought back for his ministry.
G0327.portee: This word invites reflection on what it costs to seek God or those He calls. The Jesus we seek is already there, engaged in His Father's business (Luke 2:49). Saul, whom we come to seek, is ready for his great ministry. Patient and attentive searching — with the certainty that one will find — is the very heart of faith.

sens: To tighten or fasten something around oneself with a belt or band
Figuratively, to prepare one's mind for action, to focus
To strengthen one's determination in facing trials
G0328.detail:
1. The word describes the action of tightening a belt around one's waist or clothing to prepare for work or effort. It is a concrete gesture: one "girds" their loins before acting, as one would before running or fighting.
2. In the Bible, this gesture becomes an image for "strengthening one's spirit" and preparing mentally. In 1 Peter 1:13, the apostle writes: "Gird up the loins of your mind" — he calls Christians to master their thoughts, to focus, and to remain vigilant in light of the grace of Christ that is coming.
3. The verb thus expresses a voluntary mobilization of one's entire being — body and spirit — to face the challenges of faith with sobriety and hope.
G0328.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἀνα (ana, "up, again") and ζώννυμι (zōnnumi, "to gird"). The root ζών refers to the belt (ζώνη) and the action of putting it on. In Hebrew, the verb חָגַר (khagar) expresses the same reality: to gird one's loins to prepare for action. It is a simple term but rich in imagery of combat and vigilance.
G0328.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 1:13. It is a call to moral and spiritual concentration: the Christian must "gird up the loins of his mind," meaning to clearly organize his thoughts around the hope in Christ. The apostle uses this compound verb (with the prefix "ana") to emphasize a renewed and energetic action. It is a typical term of New Testament parenesis (moral exhortation), which reminds us of the urgency and personal decision of the believer.
G0328.portee: For today's reader, this word invites awareness that faith is not passive: it requires active vigilance, a taking control of one's mind. This call to "gird up the loins of your mind" reminds us that following Christ demands mental clarity, sobriety, and firm intention. It is a beautiful image to show that the Christian life requires being "ready for action" spiritually.

sens: to revive a fire by rekindling it
to revive something that is weakening or has gone out
to awaken a dormant or weakened ability
to rekindle a feeling or disposition of the soul
G0329.detail:
1. The word first paints the image of a fire that is rekindled by adding fuel or blowing on it: it is relit after it has weakened. This is why Paul uses it figuratively in 2 Timothy 1:6: the gift of God that has been received is like a spark that risks going out if neglected.
2. The word applies more broadly to anything that weakens or dozes off: one can rekindle a strength, an ability, a grace received from God. It is never about creating something new, but awakening what already exists but is weakening.
3. The context of 2 Timothy 1:6 shows that what is being rekindled is an inner gift, a disposition of the spirit or heart that tends to go out. Paul urges Timothy not to let the charisma and power that the Spirit has given him at his ordination fall asleep.
4. It is a call to action: to rekindle implies that one must stir oneself, intentionally reviving what weakens, rather than letting it fade away through inertia or fear.
G0329.origine: The Greek word is composed of three elements: ana- ("again, back"), zôos ("living"), and pyr ("fire"). The image is that of a fire being rekindled. The word conveys the idea of restoring life or strength to something that is weakening. It is a vivid and familiar image: we have all seen a fire that diminishes and is rekindled by blowing on it or adding wood.
G0329.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 1:6, in a pastoral letter where Paul encourages Timothy not to neglect his ministry and the gifts that God has entrusted to him. The usage is clearly figurative: it is not a material fire that is being rekindled, but the grace, power, or spiritual anointing that God has given to Timothy at his commissioning. Paul suggests that this grace can weaken, doze off, and must be rekindled through faith, obedience, and commitment. It is a call to vigilance and steadfastness in the Christian life and service.
G0329.portee: This word speaks to the heart of every Christian: it reminds us that the gifts and grace that God gives us are not a passive possession, but something we must maintain and rekindle. If we neglect them out of fear, laziness, or discouragement, they weaken. Paul's call to Timothy is also a call for us: it is a reminder of our responsibility to actively cultivate our faith, our gifts, and our commitment to God, rather than letting them slowly extinguish.

sens: to revive, to be reborn
to restore an expression of feeling or friendship that had weakened
G0330.detail:
1. The word evokes the image of a plant that greens again after winter, or a flame that is relit: it is to bring back to life what had fallen asleep or weakened. In Philippians 4:10, Paul says that the Philippians have "renewed" their attention towards him — not that they had forgotten him, but their active concern for him had dozed off, and now it comes back to life.
2. The word precisely designates the resumption, the restoration of a relationship or feeling. The Philippians thought of Paul, but without being able to express it; now that the opportunity arises, their affection blooms and expresses itself again. It is less about "inventing something new" than "rekindling the existing."
G0330.origine: The word is composed of the prefix *ana* ("again", "back") and *thallō* ("to bloom", "to prosper"). It literally paints a flowering that begins again. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament uses related verbs to say that vegetation comes back to life (like *pāraḥ*, "to flourish" in Ezekiel 17:24) or that joy bursts forth (*ālaz*, "to exult").
G0330.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Philippians 4:10. Paul uses it to praise the Philippians for having rekindled their concern for him through their offering and news. It is a delicate way of saying: you had the desire, you did not have the opportunity, but now you have seized it. The verb expresses less guilt than the joy of resumption.
G0330.portee: This word soothes the heart of the Christian who fears having forgotten or abandoned a friend, a commitment, a prayer. It says that rekindling a sincere affection is a true good, and that dormant love is not dead: it just needs an opportunity to bloom again. It is a promise of a second chance.

sens: a religious offering dedicated to God
a thing or person devoted to destruction by divine order
a curse, a solemn imprecation
a spiritual condemnation, an exclusion from communion
a formula of excommunication or rejection
G0331.detail:
1. In Greek paganism, a religious offering placed in a temple as a sign of devotion to the gods. This meaning appears in votive objects: consecrated objects in homage.

2. In the Old Testament, a thing or person entirely devoted to God, often to be destroyed or set apart (like a conquered city that was entirely delivered to divine judgment). This is the meaning of the Hebrew word "herem."

3. A solemn curse pronounced against someone, with the personal commitment to curse oneself if one does not keep their word. In Acts 23:14, the conspirators bind themselves "by imprecations against themselves," meaning they agree to become anathema if they do not kill Paul.

4. The divine judgment that strikes one who rejects faith in Christ. In 1 Corinthians 12:3, to say "Jesus is anathema" means to curse or reject him; it is the exact opposite of confessing him as Lord. In Romans 9:3, Paul uses the word to express his distress: he would wish to take upon himself the curse of separation from Christ to save his unbelieving brothers.

5. The final condemnation and separation from God. In 1 Corinthians 16:22 and Galatians 1:8-9, anyone who rejects the Gospel or the person of the Lord deserves to be struck with anathema: they are delivered to divine judgment.
G0331.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "anatithémi" ("to place upon", "to dedicate"). Originally, it designated any object that was "placed" in a temple as an offering to the gods. When the Greek translators of the Old Testament encountered the Hebrew word "herem" ("forbidden", "devoted to destruction"), they rendered it as "anathema", thus transforming a concept of positive consecration into divine judgment. The word therefore retains both the idea of devotion to God and that of radical separation.
G0331.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, always to express a rupture with God or a solemn curse. In Acts 23:14, it designates the imprecation by which the Jews bind themselves not to eat until they have killed Paul. In Romans 9:3, Paul uses the word to express the extreme distress of one who would wish to sacrifice himself for the salvation of his brothers. In 1 Corinthians 12:3 and 16:22, as well as in Galatians 1:8-9, "anathema" is the formula of condemnation against those who deny the Lord Jesus or preach another Gospel. It is a term of finality, total exclusion: to be anathema means to be rejected by God and His people.
G0331.portee: This word reminds the Christian of the gravity of faith in Jesus Christ and the importance of fidelity to the Gospel. It is not an indifferent matter: confessing Jesus as Lord or denying him determines our relationship with God. The word also expresses the moral distress of the believer in the face of the unbelief of his brothers (Romans 9:3) and the urgency of remaining steadfast in the truth of the Gospel against false teachers (Galatians 1:8-9). It is a call to spiritual clarity and discernment.

sens: To cast curses or imprecations upon oneself
To commit by oath, invoking a curse if one fails to keep the promise
To swear by dedicating oneself to destruction if one does not keep one's word
G0332.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of casting curses or imprecations upon oneself — that is, wishing harm upon one's own person. This is what Peter does in Mark 14:71, when he swears and casts imprecations while denying knowing Jesus: he calls a curse upon himself to give weight to his oath.
2. More broadly, it is an act by which one commits under oath, invoking a curse: one binds oneself by a promise reinforced by the threat of divine punishment. The men in Acts 23:12 "bound themselves with imprecations" to fast until they had killed Paul: they swear to do it, and if they fail to keep this oath, misfortune would fall upon the perjurer.
3. It is therefore also to dedicate oneself to destruction conditionally: if there is no fulfillment, let me be cursed. This formula makes the oath irrevocable and solemn.
G0332.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and combines the prefix ἀνα- ("again," "upward") with θεματίζω (related to θέμα, "that which is placed"). It is formed from ἀνάθεμα, which means "anathema" or "thing devoted to destruction." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the corresponding word is חָרַם (ḥaram, "devote to destruction"), found in solemn vows where one binds oneself by a curse to guarantee one's word.
G0332.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in contexts of solemn oath. In Mark 14:71, Peter casts imprecations upon himself while denying knowing Jesus, thus amplifying his lie with a false oath. In the three passages of Acts 23:12, 14, and 21, Jews bind themselves by this same type of cursed oath, promising to kill Paul: it is a very serious commitment where one accepts that the curse will fall upon oneself if one fails. The context shows that this practice was common among Jews to give a nearly magical force to a promise or an oath.
G0332.portee: This word reminds us of the importance that the ancients attributed to the committed word: one could only reinforce it by accepting to be cursed oneself if one violated it. For the Christian, this shows the seriousness of Peter's lie, compounded by a false oath, and the intensity of the religious fanaticism that drives the Jews in Acts to bind themselves by these imprecations. It is a lesson on the power and weight of our words: our yes and our no should suffice, without needing to call a curse upon ourselves.

sens: To observe, to look closely
To examine carefully, to meditate on something
G0333.detail:
1. To observe, to look closely: it is primarily to see something while taking the time to look at it well, like Paul who walks through the city of Athens and examines the religious altars and statues attentively (Acts 17:23). The verb suggests a sustained gaze that focuses on the details.
2. To examine carefully, to meditate on something: it goes further and reflects on what has been seen, weighing its meaning and consequences. The author of Hebrews invites his readers to consider the life and death of their spiritual leaders, that is, to study them, to meditate on them to draw a lesson of faith (Hebrews 13:7).
G0333.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ana- ("up," "again") and theōreō ("to look," "to contemplate"). This root theōreō suggests a theatrical or thoughtful observation, like an attentive spectator. The addition of ana- reinforces the idea of a complete vision, that goes up and down, examining all aspects. It is a word formed to express not a simple glance, but a serious and deliberate examination.
G0333.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 17:23, Paul uses it to describe his approach in Athens: he has "considered" the objects of Athenian devotion, in other words, he has observed the altars and religious monuments attentively and methodically. In Hebrews 13:7, the same verb is used to exhort Christians to "consider" the end of life of their spiritual leaders, that is, to examine, meditate, and learn from their example. In both cases, the word denotes thoughtful observation, not a mere passing glance.
G0333.portee: This word teaches us that true understanding requires an attentive gaze and meditation: Paul does not simply pass through Athens with his eyes closed; he observes and reflects; we are similarly invited to pause on the lives of those who have gone before us in faith, to learn from their example. It is a call not to live distractedly, but to pay attention to the things of God and the witnesses of faith.

sens: precious gift dedicated to God and placed in a temple
gift made to God in fulfillment of a vow
valuable object adorning a place of worship
G0334.detail:
1. A votive offering is a sumptuous gift that a believer makes to God and places in the temple to honor Him or to fulfill a vow — in reward for a favor received or in gratitude. In Luke 21:5, Jesus looks at the beautiful stones of the temple and the magnificent offerings that adorned it: objects of gold, silver, or bronze that the faithful had brought.
2. This gift can also be a crafted object placed in fulfillment of a promise made to God — for example, one who has vowed to offer something to the Lord if he receives grace. The votive offering seals this vow and becomes a visible testimony of the donor's piety.
3. By extension, it is an ornament of the sanctuary: these offerings, gathered over time, beautified the temple and testified to the generosity and devotion of believers toward God.
G0334.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to offer" or "to raise up." It is from the same family as other words designating offerings and consecrations addressed to God. In the Greek Bible of the Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word meaning what is consecrated or devoted to the Lord. The basic image is that of offering something precious by placing it before God.
G0334.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 21:5. It is a traditional term that recalls the practices of the worship of the temple of Israel.
