When Jesus and His disciples admire the architectural beauty of the temple and its sacred ornaments — these consecrated offerings that made it splendid — it contrasts sharply with His immediate warning: this temple will be completely destroyed. Jesus thus redirects the gaze from the material and temporary glory of the building to what remains eternal.
G0334.portee: This word reminds us that true worship is expressed through giving and generosity toward God. But the scene in Luke 21 also warns: beautiful religious structures, even majestic ones, can disappear. What truly matters is the consecration of the heart to God, far beyond visible offerings and edifices.

sens: Persistent and shameless insistence towards someone
Lack of modesty or embarrassment in disturbing
G0335.detail:
1. The word refers to a repeated and burdensome request made without being deterred. It is the attitude of one who insists on getting what they want, regardless of the inconvenience caused. In Luke 11:8, the friend who knocks at the door at midnight to ask for bread demonstrates such insistence: he keeps coming back, unashamed to disturb, until he gets what he asks for.
2. Underlying this importunity is a lack of shame or restraint. It is to disregard the comfort of the other, continuing to disturb despite refusal or silence. The word emphasizes the lack of modesty of one who dares to insist without being discouraged.
G0335.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "without" combined with the term for "modesty" or "respect for others." It literally describes the absence of that natural restraint which prevents us from being bothersome. It is the opposite of modesty and discretion.
G0335.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:8, in the parable of the importunate friend. Jesus uses it to explain why the sleeping friend will eventually get up and give food to the one who insists: not out of friendship, but to escape this continual importunity. The context shows that Jesus values this respectful insistence — not dishonesty, but shameless perseverance — as a model for how we should pray to God.
G0335.portee: This parable reveals that God is not irritated by our repeated and sincere requests. Some "importunity" in prayer — that is, perseverance and boldness in continually returning — pleases God much more than timid restraint. The word teaches us that true faith dares to disturb God, confident that He will answer us.

sens: The act of killing someone, violent homicide
Approval, consent to a murderous act
G0336.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the act of taking life, killing someone violently — a homicide. In Acts 8:1, Saul approved of the murder of Stephen, the first Christian martyr stoned by the crowd: the word encompasses here the crime, the murderous act itself.
2. By extension, the word can also mean approval, consent to this violent act. In Acts 22:20, Paul speaks of his past: "I joined my approval to that of others" in the murder of Stephen. Here, the word captures less the homicide itself than the agreement of the spectator, their complicit consent to the death of another.
G0336.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀναιρέω (anaïreo), which means "to take away, to remove, to eliminate" — literally "to take up" (ἀνά = up, αἱρέω = to take). This basic image (to take, to remove) has specialized to denote the act of taking life, of killing. The Greek Old Testament uses this term to translate Hebrew words concerning violent death, notably הָרַג ("to kill," Numbers 11:15).
G0336.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the book of Acts and both related to the death of Stephen. These two uses show an important nuance: in Acts 8:1, it refers to the murder itself (the brutal action), while in Acts 22:20, it describes the approval, the consent of the complicit witness. The context is always serious — it is never an ordinary or just death, but a shocking homicide, a killing remembered with horror or regretted for past complicity.
G0336.portee: For the Christian reader, this word recalls the cost of rejecting the Gospel: the violent persecution of the early disciples. More intimately, it invites us to ask whether we are sometimes, like young Saul, complicit through our silence or indifference to injustice. It is a word that calls for conversion: Saul himself, recalling his "participation" in the murder of Stephen, acknowledges his past guilt and transformation.

sens: to take away, to lift up
to remove, to eliminate (something)
to cause to die, to kill (a person)
G0337.detail:
1. The primary, very concrete meaning is "to take away" or "to lift up": it is the image of a hand that takes and raises something. Acts 7:21 illustrates this when it says that Moses, "exposed" (that is, abandoned), was taken in by Pharaoh's daughter — the word first denotes this act of taking.
2. From there derives the meaning "to remove, to eliminate," applied to both abstract and concrete things: to abolish a law, to annihilate a work. In Hebrews 10:9, it refers to abolishing ("removing") the first order to establish the second.
3. Applied to people, the verb means "to cause to die, to kill." This is the dominant meaning in Acts: Herod ordered the killing of the children (Matthew 2:16), the apostles were nearly killed by the authorities (Acts 5:33), Saul persecuted Christians until he caused them to die (Acts 9:24, 22:20). Jesus was put to death by the hands of the wicked (Acts 2:23), and Stephen was killed (Acts 22:20).
G0337.origine: The word is composed of ἀνα (ana, "up, again") and αἱρέω (haireō, "to take, to remove"). The basic image is therefore "to take up," which has given rise to "to remove, to eliminate." The Greek verb often translates the Hebrew word הָרַג (harag, "to kill") in the Greek Old Testament, showing how a concrete verb of movement could acquire the meaning of a voluntary and violent action against a person.
G0337.emploi: The verb appears 23 times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts (19 occurrences). It is first used in the literal sense "to take away" (Acts 7:21: Moses exposed and taken in). But its primary usage is violent elimination: the massacre of the children (Matthew 2:16), murderous plots against Jesus (Luke 22:2, 23:32) and the apostles (Acts 5:33-36, 9:23-24), the execution of James (Acts 12:2) and Stephen (Acts 22:20), the plots against Paul (Acts 9:23-24, 23:15, 23:21). It also denotes the work of suppressing evil by Christ at the end of times (2 Thessalonians 2:8). The word retains a nuance of voluntary and often official action.
G0337.portee: This verb reminds the Christian reader of the gravity of martyrdom: the Bible does not hide that the early disciples were killed for their faith. But it also shows that these murders do not surpass God's will — Jesus himself was delivered "according to the predetermined plan" (Acts 2:23). It is a word of realism and assurance: persecution is real, but God remains sovereign over history.

sens: Who has committed no fault, no crime
Who does not deserve reproach or condemnation
Who is not guilty before the law
Exempt from guilt
G0338.detail:
1. The word literally designates one who has not committed the fault or crime of which they are accused. In Matthew 12:7, Jesus refers to the disciples as innocent, because they have not violated any true divine law by picking heads of grain on the Sabbath — they have committed no moral fault.

2. It also refers to one who does not deserve the condemnation or punishment that one would wish to impose on them. In Matthew 12:5, the priests technically violate the Sabbath in the temple without being guilty, because the law itself permits them to do so — they do not commit a blameworthy violation.

3. The term can denote the absence of guilt before the law or justice: one who has done nothing that justifies a condemnation.
G0338.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and is composed of the privative prefix "an-" (meaning "without") and an element related to guilt or fault. It is the opposite of being guilty. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "naki" (pure, exempt, not guilty), which regularly appears to designate one whose blood is innocent or who has not committed a fault.
G0338.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew 12:5-7, in a controversy about the Sabbath. Jesus defends his disciples who picked heads of grain on the Sabbath: he calls them innocent (v. 7) and illustrates that even the priests of the temple violate the Sabbath without becoming guilty (v. 5), because they obey a higher law. The context is that of the application of the law: to be innocent means that, even if one has technically broken a rule, one is not guilty because a higher requirement (mercy) prevails.
G0338.portee: This word reminds the reader that there is a crucial difference between violating the letter of a rule and being truly guilty. Jesus uses it to teach that true justice is not about mechanical obedience, but about seeking what pleases God — mercy towards others. This invites the Christian to distinguish between real guilt before God and the accusations of mere legalism.

sens: to take a sitting position, to rise up to sit
to regain consciousness and sit up (especially after death or sleep)
G0339.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply the physical action of sitting: moving from a lying or standing position to a sitting position. This is what the son of the widow of Nain does when Jesus raises him: "And the dead man sat up and began to speak" (Luke 7:15), showing through this natural gesture that he has truly returned to life.
2. The verb takes on a stronger meaning when it describes someone who regains consciousness after death or fainting. When Tabitha, raised by Peter, "opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up" (Acts 9:40), this gesture signifies much more than simple movements: it is the sign that she has regained life and her abilities. The image is one of uprightness, of returning to a living and active state.
G0339.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "ana" (upward, again) and "kathizō" (to sit, to cause to sit). This composition reinforces the idea of uprightness or returning to a sitting position. The simple verb "kathizō" is very common in the New Testament to express the action of sitting or causing someone to sit. The preposition "ana" at the beginning adds the idea of an action that is done "upward" or "again," which explains why the word is particularly used to describe someone who sits up.
G0339.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in miraculous contexts of resurrection or return to life. In Luke 7:15, it describes the widow's son who comes back to life during his resurrection by Jesus. In Acts 9:40, Tabitha sits up after being raised by Peter's prayer. These two uses, in the Gospels and Acts, mark decisive moments where death is defeated and life is restored. The word "sit" translates the Hebrew that often speaks of the transition from lying down to sitting up, a vivid image of restoration.
G0339.portee: This verb shows us how resurrection is not invisible or abstract: it manifests in the body, in the concrete gesture of someone who sits up. It is a reminder that Christ brings real people back to life, in their bodies and presence, and that resurrection is not a disappearance but a return to active life. This detail helps the reader to believe that the resurrections reported in the Bible are not visions or dreams, but real events where the dead truly rise.

sens: To make something old or worn new again
To restore something to its original state
G0340.detail:
1. Renewing means making something new again, giving new life to what has become old or decrepit. The image is that of something being rejuvenated, made capable of functioning again. In Hebrews 6:6, Paul speaks of those who "are renewed": he describes the divine action that would revive someone's faith who has fallen far from God, just as one would restore a dilapidated building.
2. Renewing can also mean restoring to the original state, returning to the original freshness. This is why the Psalms speak of God renewing the face of the earth or the breath of creatures: he restores them to their original beauty and vitality.
G0340.origine: The Greek word ἀνακαινίζω is composed of ἀνα ("again, back") and καινίζω ("to make new"), itself derived from καινός ("new"). The starting image is that of renewal, rejuvenation. In Hebrew, the original text often uses חָדַשׁ ("to renew"), showing that this concept is at the heart of biblical thought: God has the power to restore what seems lost.
G0340.emploi: The verb ἀνακαινίζω appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Hebrews 6:6. It designates the hypothetical action of "renewing" someone who has fallen from grace. The author of Psalm 103 and other psalms uses the corresponding Hebrew verb to speak of the renewal of creatures by God. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this word translates the Hebrew חָדַשׁ several times, notably in Chronicles where King Asa "renews" the covenant with the Lord.
G0340.portee: This word reminds the believer that spiritual renewal, restoration after a fall, is a real and possible divine work. It also raises the serious question posed in Hebrews 6: is it possible to return to repentance after having seriously offended God? Meditating on this term invites us to take seriously both God's grace and the gravity of our commitment to Him.

sens: Make new, restore what wears out or ages
Transform internally by restoring spiritual vigor
Reconstitute according to the divine image
G0341.detail:
1. The word expresses the action of making new what is damaged or exhausted: it is like rejuvenating something. In 2 Corinthians 4:16, the Apostle Paul describes how our inner man is renewed day by day, while our body ages and deteriorates — the image is one of daily spiritual restoration, contrasting with physical wear and tear.

2. This renewal is a profound transformation of the being, a regeneration from within. In Colossians 3:10, it refers to the result of "putting on the new man": the believer who appropriates the life of Christ is gradually transformed, becoming like the one who created him — it is a continuous process of moral and spiritual improvement.

3. This renewal is never isolated; it occurs "in knowledge," meaning it is accompanied by a growing understanding of God and His will. It restores the believer according to his original model: the image of God within him, which sin had tarnished.
G0341.origine: The Greek word is based on the prefix "ana-" (again, upward) and "kainoō" (to make new, from the word "kainos," new). The starting image is that of restoration or resurrection to a better condition. This verb is closely related to the words "kainos" (new) and "neos" (new), which run throughout the New Testament to speak of the transformation that Christ brings.
G0341.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Greek New Testament, exclusively in Paul. In 2 Corinthians 4:16, it describes the daily spiritual renewal of the believer, contrasting with the gradual destruction of the body: it is the invisible work of the Holy Spirit in the inner person. In Colossians 3:10, it is part of the exhortation to put on the new man, created according to God: renewal is presented as a continuous process (present participle in Greek) of transformation in the knowledge of God. In both contexts, it is a progressive and spiritual restoration, not an instantaneous overhaul.
G0341.portee: This word assures the believer that, even though the body ages and weakens, the inner life can be renewed daily by the grace of God. It reminds us that true Christian life is a continuous transformation, day by day, that gradually makes us conform to the image of God. It is a promise: physical fatigue and temporal exhaustion are not the final word; the Spirit continually renews the soul.

sens: Action of making new what was worn out or corrupted
Profound transformation of the spirit and mind
Restoration of creation through divine intervention
G0342.detail:
1. Renewal is the action of making new what has degraded or worn out — like renovating an old house. It is an active process where something changes state to return to a better or original form. In Titus 3:5, it is the renewal of the Holy Spirit that saves, restoring the bond between God and man.

2. This word also refers to the inner transformation of our thoughts and worldview. In Romans 12:2, Paul calls Christians to a renewal of the mind (the noûs, the faculty of thinking and judging) — not a mere superficial reform, but a complete overhaul of our way of understanding and discerning the will of God.

3. On a broader level, it is the restoration and fulfillment of creation itself, the fact that God makes all things new in His plan of salvation. Renewal is the fruit of divine grace: it is God who renews, but man cooperates by accepting this transformation.
G0342.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀνακαινόω (anakainoô), which literally means "to make anew": the preposition ἀνά (ana, "again") + καινός (kainos, "new, fresh"). It describes not just a repair (like patching a garment), but a complete renovation, a return to radical newness. The root καιν- (kaïn-) is also found in καινὴ διαθήκη (new covenant) or the Καινὸς Κόσμος (new world) of Christian eschatology.
G0342.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 12:2, it describes the renewal of the mind that believers must seek to discern the will of God — it is a personal and intellectual transformation. In Titus 3:5, it refers to the renewal of the Holy Spirit in the context of salvation: God saves us not by our merits, but by His mercy, through baptism (which symbolizes regeneration) and the renewal of the Spirit. In both cases, renewal is a salvific or transformative action operated or permitted by God.
G0342.portee: This word teaches that the Christian life is not a mere moral improvement, but a profound and radical transformation of the heart and mind. It calls us to let God renew our way of seeing the world, away from the values of the present age. It is a call to inner metamorphosis, the only means to truly discern and live the will of God in our daily lives.

sens: Remove a veil, take away what covers
Reveal, make known what was hidden
In particular: remove the obstacle that prevents seeing or understanding spiritual realities
G0343.detail:
1. The literal sense is to remove a veil or cloth that covers something. In 2 Corinthians 3:14, Paul speaks of the veil of Moses that "does not lift" when the Jews read the Old Testament: this veil is the misunderstanding that persists because they do not see that the Old Covenant finds its fulfillment in Christ.
2. In a figurative sense, to unveil means to reveal, to uncover a hidden reality or mystery. It is to remove what obstructs knowledge.
3. This is particularly the case when God removes the veils that hide spiritual realities: in 2 Corinthians 3:18, we behold "the unveiled face" of the glory of the Lord, unobstructed, directly and transformatively.
G0343.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἀνα- (upward, back) and καλύπτω (to cover, to veil). It literally means "to cover back" or "to remove the veil." The Greek word often translates the Hebrew גָּלָה (galah), which also means "to reveal" or "to uncover," particularly in the sense of unfolding what was secret or hidden.
G0343.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two given occurrences. In 2 Corinthians 3:14, it refers to the veil that covers the understanding of the Old Covenant for those who do not recognize Christ. In 2 Corinthians 3:18, it describes the condition of the believer who contemplates God without a veil interposed: his face is not covered, he sees face to face, progressively transformed from glory to glory. These two uses show how Christ removes the obstacles to the spiritual vision of God's realities.
G0343.portee: This word reminds the believer of a transforming truth: in Christ, the veils that hid the face of God fall away. We no longer see Him through shadows and figures, but directly, and this vision changes us. It invites us to pray that the veils of our own misunderstandings and unbeliefs be removed, so that we too may behold the glory of the Lord and be transformed.

sens: To go back to the place from which one departed
To return to a person or a reality
To turn away from what one had undertaken
To go back spiritually or morally
G0344.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of geographical movement: to return to the starting point. The Magi in Matthew 2:12 "return" to their country by another way after worshiping Jesus — they go back to their distant home.

2. The word also means to return to a person or a state. In Acts 18:21, Paul promises to "return" to the Ephesians, meaning to go back to see them. The peace of the disciples "returns" to them in Luke 10:6 if it does not find a child of peace — it is brought back to them, like something that reverberates.

3. It is used figuratively to mean going back on a decision, renouncing a project. The Hebrew patriarchs would have had "the time to return" to the land from which they came (Hebrews 11:15) — that is, to turn back and abandon their quest for the promised land.

4. Spiritually, this return can signify moral regression or apostasy: going back to the old life, to idolatry, to the old paths — it is the image of turning one's foot away from the way of the Lord.
G0344.origine: The Greek word combines ἀνά ("back, upward") and κάμπτω ("to bend, to curve"). The image is of one who bends their path to go back, who turns to return to the starting point. It is a neutral word, without emotional charge: it simply describes the movement of return. The Septuagint uses it to translate Hebrew verbs of return (שׁוּב, "to return," and סוּר, "to turn away").
G0344.emploi: The verb appears four times in the provided New Testament, in both senses: physical return and figurative return. Matthew 2:12 and Hebrews 11:15 express a concrete return to the place of origin (the Magi to the East, the patriarchs to Mesopotamia). Acts 18:21 and Luke 10:6 use it in a more metaphorical or spiritual way — the former for a promise of a future visit, the latter for the return of an immaterial reality (peace). No usage carries condemnation: it is a descriptive term, which can denote a good return (that of the Magi) or a rejected return (that of the patriarchs to Ur).
G0344.portee: This verb reminds the reader that the disciple's path is not a simple accomplishment, but a progress that requires turning one's back on the past. Knowing that there is always the possibility to "return" — as the patriarchs could have done — challenges faith: should one persevere or abandon? It is an invitation to hold firm in the promise, without nostalgia for the "onions of Egypt." At the same time, the word opens up hope: Jesus will also "return," an awaited and glorious return.

sens: To take a reclining or semi-reclining position to eat and drink
To be among the guests at a meal
To participate in a table communion, an intimacy of sharing bread
G0345.detail:
1. In antiquity, people did not sit on chairs to eat: they reclined on beds arranged around a low table, propped up on one elbow, with their bodies relaxed. The verb precisely describes this reclining posture. In Mark 14:18, during the Last Supper, Jesus and his disciples are "at table" in this traditional position when one of them is about to betray him.
2. The word also simply denotes being present at a meal as a guest, without emphasizing the posture. In Matthew 9:10, many tax collectors come to "sit at table" with Jesus: it is an action of participation, of joining the group of eaters.
3. By extension, "to be at table" evokes intimacy and acceptance: eating together was an act loaded with social and spiritual significance. In Luke 22:27, Jesus reminds that he is "at table" as one who serves, transforming the meal into an image of humility and love.
G0345.origine: The Greek word ἀνάκειμαι comes from ἀνά ("upward, again") and κεῖμαι ("to lie down, to be laid"). The basic image is therefore that of a body lying down. In the late Greek of the New Testament, it has almost replaced κεῖσθαι and κατακεῖσθαι (which also mean "to lie down") to specifically designate the posture of the guest during the meal. This nuance reflects the living context of the early Christians.
G0345.emploi: The verb appears 14 times in the Gospels, never in the epistles. It is very frequent in meal scenes: in Matthew 9:10 and 22:10-11, Jesus eats with tax collectors or at the wedding of the king's son; in Mark 14:18 and parallels, during the Last Supper, the disciples are "at table" when Jesus announces his betrayal. In John, the participle ἀνακείμενος emphasizes the state of one who rests at table: in John 13:23, the beloved disciple is reclining next to Jesus' breast, a poignant image of intimacy. The word does not vary much: it is always the posture and presence of the eater at the moment of the meal that matters.
G0345.portee: For the Christian reader, this word roots the Gospel in concrete reality: Jesus eats, he rests at table like any man. But he also transforms the meal into a theological act: eating with him becomes a sign of welcome, forgiveness, and communion. Understanding that one was "reclining" at table, not sitting, helps to imagine the intimacy and vulnerability of these moments, where Jesus gives himself body and soul to his disciples and to those who were rejected.

sens: To bring together into a single whole what was dispersed or separated
To summarize in a formula or principle that encompasses everything
To recapitulate, to take back the essence of a thing
G0346.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of gathering, of bringing together scattered elements to make a coherent whole. It is an image of concentration: just as one groups pieces of a puzzle, one "gathers" what was separated. In Ephesians 1:10, Paul speaks of gathering "all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth" — the idea is that everything that exists, scattered across the corners of creation, will be brought under one head, Christ.
2. More broadly, the word can mean to summarize or recapitulate: to gather the essence of several ideas or commandments into a single formula that contains them all. This is what Paul does in Romans 13:9, where he groups all the commandments of the Law into this single principle: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
3. The word also suggests the idea of gathering to put in order, unifying what is fragmented, in order to restore original harmony and unity.
G0346.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "ana-" (again, upward) and "kephalaioo" (which comes from "kephale," the head). The basic image is therefore "to bring back to the head" or "to return to the head" — hence "to put under one head." This evokes both the action of gathering elements and that of summarizing them into a primary principle. The word expresses the biblical idea that all things converge towards a central point, a supreme unity.
G0346.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 13:9, Paul uses it to show how all the commandments of the Mosaic Law boil down to the love of neighbor. In Ephesians 1:10, he refers to God's great plan to gather under the authority of Christ all creation, heavenly and earthly, at the culmination of the ages. In both cases, the word expresses the idea of unification or recapitulation: bringing diversity to unity, the many to the one, all to Christ.
G0346.portee: This word reveals two truths that transform the faith of the Christian. First, it shows that God's Law, far from being an accumulation of arbitrary rules, is summarized in a single love: to love God and neighbor. Secondly, it reminds us that the history of the world is not chaos, but a movement towards a recapitulation in Christ, where all things will find their place and meaning. This invites the Christian to see their life not as a succession of scattered events, but as part of a grand design of unification in Jesus Christ.

sens: To be reclining or lying on a couch, especially during a meal
To sit or lie down to eat, to take a place at the table
To place someone in a reclining or sitting position
To settle a child down for rest
G0347.detail: 1. The verb first evokes the concrete image of leaning back or stretching out on a low couch used at meals: this is the posture of the ancient guest who eats while reclining or semi-reclining on a couch (Matthew 8:11, 14:19). 2. More broadly, it means to be seated or to be placed at the table to share a meal: in the kingdom of heaven, the righteous "will be at the table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (Matthew 8:11), and the happy master "will have them recline at the table" to serve them (Luke 12:37). 3. The verb is also used to place someone in a position of rest or relaxation: to have a crowd "sit down in groups on the green grass" to feed them (Mark 6:39). 4. It can denote the simple action of laying someone down, without the idea of a meal: Mary "laid" her newborn son "in a manger" (Luke 2:7), an act of maternal tenderness.
G0347.origine: The word is formed from the prefix ἀνα- ("upward, backward") and the verb κλίνω ("to lean, to bend"). The basic image is that of the body leaning or lying back. In ancient Greek, to recline at a meal literally meant to stretch out on a low couch (the klinē), a Mediterranean custom quite different from our modern chairs. This posture was a sign of freedom and status: only free and honored men took their meals reclining.
G0347.emploi: The verb appears six times in the Gospels, always in the present or aorist tense. It focuses on two main uses: first, being seated or reclining at the table for a meal (Matthew 8:11, 14:19; Luke 12:37; Luke 13:29), a powerful image of the feast of the kingdom of God where the righteous are served by Christ himself; secondly, placing or laying someone in a position of rest (Mark 6:39 for seating the crowd, Luke 2:7 for laying down the Child Jesus). The context varies: ordinary meals, the miracle of multiplication, the birth of the Savior, the promise of future judgment. The meaning nuances according to the object: it is an honor at the table, a convenience for sitting, a care for a newborn.
G0347.portee: This verb connects the reader to the practices and living conditions of the ancient Near East, but above all, it carries a strong spiritual significance: being seated at the table with Jesus is an image of fellowship and intimacy with the Lord. The meal becomes the place of divine blessing and equality between the master and his servants. It is an invitation to understand that our status as believers places us in a position of honor before God, loved and served by Christ.

sens: To let out a sudden and violent cry
To scream in fear or surprise
To shout while speaking with force and urgency
G0349.detail:
1. To cry out means to shout suddenly and forcefully, often involuntarily. This is what the disciples do when they see Jesus walking on the sea (Mark 6:49): seized by fear, they let out involuntary cries.
2. It is also the cry of a man possessed by a spirit when he sees Jesus: he "cried out with a loud voice" (Luke 4:33), as if the creature within him reacted against its will to the presence of the Lord.
3. Finally, it is to cry out together to insist on something, like the crowd that "cried out" to demand Jesus' death (Luke 23:18): a collective and urgent cry.
G0349.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: "ana" (upward, again) and "krazo" (to cry). This root "krazo" evokes an animalistic, raw, spontaneous cry. Together, the word means primarily to cry out towards something or someone, to cry again, or to cry with intensity. Greek often translates the Hebrew word "qara" which simply means "to call" or "to cry" in the Old Testament.
G0349.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Gospels, always in Luke and Mark. It describes violent cries: those of the possessed who see Jesus (Mark 1:23, Luke 4:33, Luke 8:28), those of the disciples seized by fear (Mark 6:49), or those of the furious crowd (Luke 23:18). Each time, the cry is sudden, intense, and reveals extreme emotion — fear, urgency, or a pressing demand. It is a dramatic word that creates an atmosphere of tension in the scenes where it appears.
G0349.portee: This word shows us how cries of distress, fear, or passion arise from the depths of us, escaping our control. The possessed who cry in the presence of Jesus, the frightened disciples, the frenzied crowd — all reveal through their cries what they truly are. This invites us to ask God to purify our hearts, for our cries reveal what dwells within us.

sens: To ask someone questions to obtain information or a confession
To examine something carefully to judge its nature or value
To judge, evaluate the validity of an accusation or behavior
To question, challenge the legitimacy of something
G0350.detail:
1. To interrogate someone means to ask them questions in order to discover the truth or obtain answers. In Luke 23:14, Pilate says, "I have interrogated him before you," meaning he questioned Jesus to verify the accusations against him. In Acts 12:19, Herod interrogates the guards to find out what happened during Peter's escape. It is an act of directed, voluntary, and active inquiry.
2. To examine carefully means to scrutinize, weigh, analyze something to grasp its true nature. In Acts 17:11, the Bereans "examined the Scriptures daily," meaning they read them with critical attention to verify if the things Paul taught were true. It is the act of discernment and verification.
3. To judge something or someone means to form a judgment about its moral or factual value. In 1 Corinthians 2:14, Paul says that the natural man cannot "judge" (or evaluate) the things of the Spirit because he lacks the capacity. It is the exercise of moral or spiritual discernment.
4. To question or challenge means to raise an objection or refuse to accept without examination. In 1 Corinthians 9:3, Paul defends himself against those who accuse him: he responds to those who question his apostleship. It is reacting to a challenge with a justification.
G0350.origine: The Greek word ἀνακρίνω is composed of the prefix ἀνα- ("upward," "again," "back") and the verb κρίνω ("to judge," "to discern," "to separate"). The basic meaning is therefore: to examine deeply, scrutinizing in search of the truth. The root κρίνω literally means "to separate" or "to sort" — imagine separating the good grain from the chaff. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word often corresponds to חָקַר ("to scrutinize," "to search"), which shares this idea of a thorough inquiry. The prefix ἀνα- adds the idea of a thorough examination, from bottom to top.
G0350.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts (where it describes judicial interrogations and inquiries) and in Paul's letters (where he speaks of judgment and spiritual discernment). In the narratives of Acts, "to interrogate" is often a judicial act: authorities interrogate the apostles or witnesses to establish the facts (Acts 4:9, 12:19, 24:8, 28:18). In Paul, the meaning broadens: to interrogate or judge becomes the exercise of spiritual discernment. In 1 Corinthians 2:14-15, the contrast is striking — the carnal man cannot judge spiritual things, but he who possesses the Spirit can judge all things. In 1 Corinthians 10:25 and 10:27, "to judge" means to examine one's conscience or consult one's knowledge to act according to wisdom. The word can also mean "to accuse" or "to contest" (1 Corinthians 9:3), that is, to raise an objection against someone. The meaning always revolves around the idea of examining, testing, seeking the truth.
G0350.portee: This word invites the Christian to exercise active and vigilant discernment — not to passively accept what is taught, but to examine all things in the light of the Spirit and the Word. The Bereans (Acts 17:11) provide the model: they "examined the Scriptures" to verify the teaching received. It is a call to spiritual maturity, to personal responsibility in faith. At the same time, the word emphasizes that true judgment — that which discerns the spiritual from the carnal — belongs only to those who possess the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:15). It is thus a freedom and a responsibility, but also a grace.

sens: Investigation conducted before a judgment to establish the facts
Action of interrogating an accused person to know the truth
Judicial instruction aimed at clarifying a case
G0351.detail:
1. This word refers to the thorough examination that a magistrate must conduct before making a decision or forwarding a case to a superior. It is the preliminary investigation, the judicial instruction. In Acts 25:26, Governor Festus explains to King Agrippa that he has brought Paul before him for an "examination" of his case, to know what to write to the emperor.
2. The word concretely evokes the interrogation and investigation: the accused is questioned, testimonies and facts are examined to discern the truth. It is the process by which one comes to know the reality of a case before judging it or reporting it to a higher authority.
G0351.origine: The word comes from the verb "anakrino" which means "to examine, to interrogate, to judge." The prefix "ana-" (again, backward) suggests an investigation that goes back to the sources: one "questions" to understand well. It is a common Greek judicial term, used notably for administrative inquiries and instruction procedures.
G0351.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 25:26). It is a technical term from Roman and Greek legal vocabulary. In this context, Festus, the Roman governor of Judea, uses it to refer to the examination he must conduct on Paul before presenting him to Caesar. The preliminary investigation was an essential step in the judicial process: it allowed authorities to gather the necessary information before rendering judgment or forwarding the case to a higher court.
G0351.portee: This word reminds us that true justice rests on a thorough investigation and an honest examination of the facts. For the believer, it emphasizes the importance of seeking the truth before judging, and not being influenced by appearances or unfounded accusations. Paul, being examined publicly before the king, benefits from this judicial instruction that protects the innocent.

sens: To stand up, to be upright after being bent or stooped
To lift one's head, to look upward
To regain confidence, to recover morally
G0352.detail:
1. The literal sense is physical: to raise one's body that was bent or stooped forward. The woman in Luke 13:11 was "bent over" for eighteen years due to an infirmity, and she "could not straighten up at all" — the verb denotes the action of regaining an upright posture.

2. To lift one's head also means to raise one's gaze upward, a natural gesture that often accompanies the raising of the body. When Jesus says in Luke 21:28, "stand up and lift your heads," he encourages his disciples not to remain crushed by fear, but to look up with confidence.

3. In a moral sense, to straighten up can express the act of regaining assurance or dignity. In John 8:7, Jesus rises from the position where he was crouched down writing: it is a gesture that marks his mastery and resolution before facing his accusers. The raising of the body then becomes a sign of regained inner strength.
G0352.origine: The verb is composed of the prefix ana- ("upward, backward") and kuptō ("to bend, to incline"). The starting image is very concrete: it is the opposite movement of bending, straightening what was bent or stooped. In ancient Hebrew, the verb נָשָׂא (nassa, "to lift, to carry") sometimes conveys this same idea of lifting the head or body.
G0352.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, always in Luke or in the Gospel of John, and always in scenes of bodily movement. In Luke 13:11, it describes the handicap of a woman who cannot straighten up. In Luke 21:28, Jesus uses it in the future as a call to confidence in the face of end-time events. In John 8:7 and 8:10, it reports the gestures of Jesus during the judgment of the adulterous woman: he straightens up to speak. In each context, the straightening of the body is linked to an inner state — infirmity, fear, or on the contrary assurance and dignity.
G0352.portee: This word reminds us that our physical posture and our spiritual attitude are linked. A woman bent over for eighteen years could not lift her eyes or look ahead; when Jesus heals her, she straightens up. For the believer, "to straighten up" in faith means to reject shame, fear, or discouragement, and to look toward the hope of God. It is also a call to the dignity that Jesus restores in each one.

sens: Lift or carry something from the ground
Take something or someone with oneself
Take or lead someone
Put on or equip oneself with something
Ascend to heaven, rise up
G0353.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to lift something, to raise it: one takes an object and carries it. In Acts 7:43, the Israelites "carried" the tent of Moloch, meaning they transported it with them as an object of worship.
2. To take something or someone with oneself, to welcome: in Acts 20:14, the disciples "take" Paul aboard the boat to travel together.
3. To take or lead: in Acts 23:31, the soldiers take Paul at night to lead him to Caesarea by placing him on a horse.
4. To put on or equip oneself, as one would with armor: in Ephesians 6:13 and 6:16, one "takes" the full armor of God and the shield of faith to protect oneself spiritually.
5. To ascend to heaven, to rise up: Jesus was "taken up" to heaven (Mark 16:19, Acts 1:11), an image of his glorious ascension after his resurrection.
G0353.origine: The word comes from the Greek ana- ("upward, again") and lambanō ("to take, seize"). The basic image is therefore to "take upward" or to "lift." In the Greek Old Testament, this word primarily translates the Hebrew verb nasa ("to bear, lift") and sometimes laqah ("to take"), words that share this same idea of movement or seizing.
G0353.emploi: This word appears about 13 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Acts and the Pauline epistles. In Acts 1 and 16, "remove" refers to Jesus' ascension to heaven, a key moment of his return to the Father. In Acts 20 and 23, "take" has an everyday sense: taking someone aboard, putting them on a horse. In Ephesians 6, "taking" the armor of God is a call to action for the believer to prepare for spiritual battle. In 1 Timothy 3:16, Jesus is "taken up" in glory, another reference to his ascension. The word oscillates between the concrete (transporting an object or a person) and the spiritual (being received in heaven).
G0353.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that Jesus' ascension is not a disappearance, but an exaltation: he was received in heaven as the glorified Lord. Figuratively, "taking the armor of God" invites the believer to actively seize the spiritual resources that God offers against evil. It is a call to move from passivity to action in one's faith life.

sens: Action of taking someone from one place to another
Passage of a person from earth to heaven
Ascension of Jesus to heaven after his resurrection
G0354.detail:
1. The word literally describes the action of taking someone, of taking them to transport them elsewhere. It is a movement upward, a departure. In Luke 9:51, it refers to the moment when Jesus will be taken from the earth: "When the time came for him to be taken up from the world."

2. More broadly, this term refers to the passage of a person from earth to heaven, not by ordinary death, but by a divine action that carries them away. It is a superhuman act of God who takes someone and transports them to heaven.

3. For Jesus, this word names his ascension: after his resurrection, he is taken from the presence of the disciples and ascends to heaven. It is not a simple disappearance, but a voluntary and glorious elevation to the Father.
G0354.origine: The word comes from the verb "analambanô" (to take, remove, carry) formed from "ana" (upward, again) and "lambano" (to take). The prefix "ana" gives the idea of upward movement. It is a term that evokes divine action: God taking someone to bring them back to himself, upward. The root "lambano" (to take) also appears in "lambanô" (to receive), emphasizing here an active taking.
G0354.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 9:51, to designate the moment when Jesus approaches the time of his rapture to heaven. Luke uses it when speaking of Jesus' departure to Jerusalem, where he would die and rise again before ascending to heaven. It is a solemn term that frames the entire final trajectory of Jesus: his passion, resurrection, and ascension are referred to as his "rapture." The word emphasizes that what happens is not a tragic end, but a divine act of taking and elevation.
G0354.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals that the passion and ascension of Jesus are not two separate events, but two sides of the same act: his rapture to the Father. It is a teaching of trust: Jesus' death is not a defeat, but the path to his exaltation. This word also invites the believer to see beyond the cross and the empty tomb: Jesus returns to his Father in glory.

sens: Spend, use until exhaustion
Destroy or annihilate by fire or violence
Gnaw or devour gradually
G0355.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to spend or consume a resource: to use something until nothing remains. It is the idea of a gradual expenditure that slowly empties what one possesses.

2. However, in the New Testament, the word takes on a more destructive and violent sense. In Luke 9:54, the disciples ask if Jesus wants a fire from heaven to "consume" the Samaritans — it refers to completely destroying or annihilating by flame. It is total and definitive destruction.

3. In Galatians 5:15, Paul warns the Galatians: if you bite and devour one another, you will be "destroyed" by one another. Here, the verb describes a progressive and mutual action of destruction — like animals gnawing at each other until their own ruin.
G0355.origine: The Greek word ἀναλίσκω is composed of ἀνά ("upward, again") and a root related to ἀλών or ἄλη ("to burn, consume"). The starting image is that of a flame that rises and devours. The Hebrew word אָכַל ("to eat, devour") often translates the same concept of consumption or destruction.
G0355.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the provided New Testament: once in the sense of destruction by fire (Luke 9:54, in the disciples' request), once in the sense of mutual or progressive destruction (Galatians 5:15, in Paul's warning against divisions). In both cases, it describes a total and irreversible action — either sudden and violent destruction or gradual consumption leading to ruin.
G0355.portee: This word reminds the Christian that divisions and conflicts among brothers are not trivial: they lead to mutual destruction. Paul uses it to seriously warn the Galatians that their quarrels are destroying them from within, just as fire consumes wood.

sens: Proportional relationship between two things
Harmonious correspondence between distinct elements
Conformity to a model or established rule
G0356.detail:
1. Analogy is primarily a mathematical or logical relationship of proportion: as one is to another, so this one is to that one. It is the idea of a balanced and measured relationship between two or more terms.

2. In common language, it refers to the correspondence or harmony between distinct things: they resemble each other in their structure or function, even if they are not identical.

3. In Romans 12:6, the Apostle Paul speaks of the "analogy of faith": it means that the one exercising the gift of prophecy must do so in accordance with and in harmony with the entirety of the Christian faith, without contradicting or deviating from its fundamental principles. It is an internal regulation: the gift must function in proper proportion with the whole body of doctrine.
G0356.origine: The word comes from the Greek *logos* (word, relation, reason) preceded by the prefix *ana* (again, back). The starting image is that of a calculation or a relationship: one weighs one thing against another to see if they agree. In Greek mathematics, analogy specifically referred to an equality of ratios: a is to b as c is to d. The Greek Bible uses it rarely; it is a scholarly word that occurs only once in the New Testament.
G0356.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 12:6. Paul uses it to frame the exercise of spiritual gifts, particularly prophecy. He teaches that each Christian receives different gifts according to grace, but these gifts must be employed "according to the analogy of faith." This expression means that the prophet must not invent a new or contradictory doctrine, but speak in harmony with the faith received and transmitted by the Church. It is a criterion for discernment: to verify that the manifestation of the gift aligns with the entirety of the taught revelation of God.
G0356.portee: This word reminds the Christian that the gifts of the Spirit are not given to unleash individual fantasy or unbridled personal inspiration. They must be exercised in harmony with the entire faith taught by the apostles and recorded in Scripture. It is a protection against falsehood and heresy: a prophet, a teacher, a shepherd must ensure that what he announces does not contradict the received Word. The analogy of faith is thus the principle of unity and truth for the life of the Church.

sens: Weigh a reality in one's mind to understand it and draw a lesson from it
G0357.detail: 1. To consider is to focus one's attention on something, to weigh it mentally, to reflect on it in order to grasp its meaning and draw a useful conclusion. The Greek word ἀναλογίζομαι combines the idea of "going back to" (prefix ἀνα-) and "calculation or reasoning" (λογίζ-), as if the mind were going back from observation to understanding. In Hebrews 12:3, the author exhorts Christians to "consider him who endured such opposition from sinners against himself": it is about actively meditating on the example of Jesus, fixing it in one's heart to find strength against discouragement.
G0357.origine: The Greek verb is formed from the prefix ἀνα- (to go back, to return) and λογίζ- (to count, to calculate, to reason), derived from λόγος (the word, the reason). The starting image is that of a reason that goes back, that reflects, that establishes an account. It is a word of active and intelligent meditation, very close to the French words "logarithm" or "logic," which share the same root.
G0357.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 12:3. The author of the epistle uses it to invite his persecuted readers to deeply meditate on the patience and endurance of Christ. It is a rare but powerful word, which implies a conscious effort of the mind to draw lessons from an example.
G0357.portee: This verb shows us that faith is not passive. When we are discouraged by difficulties, we are called to consider, to weigh, to meditate on the example of Christ who suffered without complaint. This active reflection becomes a source of strength and perseverance in our own journey.

sens: that has lost its salt or taste
that does not sting, that is bland
that has lost its useful effect or value
G0358.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to salt that has lost its pungent flavor, its ability to give taste. In Mark 9:50, Jesus poses this troubling question: "If the salt loses its flavor, with what will you season it?" — it is an impossibility, for salt is by nature flavorful; what can no longer serve any purpose must be thrown away.
2. Figuratively, this evokes anything that has been emptied of its substance, its zest, its effectiveness: something that should have value but no longer does. Jesus speaks of disciples who would cease to be "the salt of the earth" (Matthew 5:13).
3. The image underscores the absurdity: what good is salt that does not season? Likewise, what good is a disciple who no longer produces spiritual fruit?
G0358.origine: The word comes from the Greek "halas" (salt). In Greek, "a-nalos" literally means "without salt." It is a negative compound: the prefix "a-" (without) joined to "nalos" (salt). The image of salt holds great importance in biblical thought: salt preserves, purifies, gives flavor, symbolizes the covenant. Tasteless salt is therefore a contradiction in terms, which reinforces the strength of Jesus' words.
G0358.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 9:50. Jesus uses it in a context of moral challenge addressed to his disciples: after speaking of the cost of discipleship and the importance of not causing little ones to stumble, he calls them to be "the salt of the earth." If this salt loses its flavor — that is, if the disciple abandons his mission or integrity — he becomes useless. The idea is not that chemical salt would naturally lose its taste, but that morally and spiritually, one who should be a purifying and preserving influence can become corrupted or harmless.
G0358.portee: This word challenges the Christian reader regarding their own value and responsibility. Being a disciple means having received a mission: to preserve, season, influence the world for the Gospel. If we conform to the world instead of transforming it, if we lose our zeal or integrity, we become "tasteless" — morally and spiritually useless. It is a call to remain faithful, active, and to keep what distinguishes us as children of God.

sens: The action of detaching or separating from a place
The moment when a soul leaves life
The end of a life or presence
G0359.detail: 1. This word primarily describes the action of loosening, detaching, as when a ship is cast off from its moorings to set sail — a very concrete image of what is undone or released. 2. In the Bible, it particularly refers to the moment when the soul detaches from the body, death viewed not as a brutal end, but as a departure, a separation. Paul speaks of it this way: "the time of my departure has come" (2 Timothy 4:6), in a final letter where he calmly accepts leaving life. 3. It is a poetic and peaceful way to evoke the death of a believer — less an end than a transition, a goodbye rather than a farewell without return.
G0359.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to loosen, detach, release" (ἀναλύω). It is formed from the prefix "ana" (upward, again) and the root meaning "to tie, bind." It is in the same family as "analyze" in French — the word meaning "to decompose." The image of departure naturally comes from that of a rope being untied or a knot being undone.
G0359.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in 2 Timothy 4:6, in the second letter that the Apostle Paul writes to Timothy shortly before his death. Paul uses this image of departure to refer to the approach of his end; he speaks of himself as "being poured out as a drink offering" and that "the time of my departure has come." It is a serene, almost joyful language — Paul prepares for execution without fear, seeing his death as a release rather than a catastrophe. The word thus reveals how a mature believer views the end of life: not as destruction, but as a journey.
G0359.portee: This word teaches the reader a Christian attitude towards death: that of a peaceful transition rather than a horrifying end. Death is not annihilation, but a departure to the presence of the Lord. For Paul, approaching the end of life with this serenity — speaking of "departure" — is a testimony of solid faith in the resurrection and eternal life. It encourages the believer to view their own end not with fear, but with that same hope.

sens: To detach, to loosen from something
To leave a place to go elsewhere
To return from where one came
To die, to separate from earthly life
G0360.detail: 1. The primary meaning of the word is literally "to loosen" or "to detach" — it is the image of a rope being undone. This is why it is used to express departure: one loosens from what was holding them back. 2. When speaking of a person, it means leaving one place to go elsewhere, like a master returning from a wedding (Luke 12:36): the context suggests an absence followed by a return. 3. This word can also mean "to return to," "to go back" (Luke 12:36 translates it as "to return"), as departing often implies the idea of coming from elsewhere. 4. The deepest usage is in Philippians 1:23, where Paul speaks of "departing and being with Christ": this is the departure that constitutes death, the soul being freed from the earthly body to join the Lord.
G0360.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "ana" (upward, return) and "luô" (to loosen, detach). This combination creates the idea of a "loosening upward or backward," a departure that often brings one back. The root "luô" (to loosen) is very ancient and appears in other words expressing liberation or rupture. It is a scholarly word, quintessentially Greek, that is rarely encountered in the Greek Old Testament.
G0360.emploi: This verb appears twice in the New Testament according to the provided usages. First in Luke (12:36), it describes the master returning from the wedding: it is a return from absence. Then in Paul (Philippians 1:23), it denotes the departure from this earthly life to be with Christ: this is the strongest and most spiritual usage. The meaning thus shifts from geographical return to the definitive separation that is Christian death. Paul uses this word with an almost joyful lightness: to depart for him is a deliverance, an infinitely better presence. The context of each verse affects the nuance: in Luke, it is temporal absence; in Paul, it is the eternal absence of the body, transformed into the presence of Christ.
G0360.portee: For a Christian, this word summarizes a profound truth: death is not an absurd or terrifying end, but a departure to true presence. In Paul, it transforms mourning into hope. To depart from here is to be loosened from all that weighed us down — not as an escape, but as a liberation. This word also invites not to become permanently attached to this world: we are in waiting, like the master of the servants in Luke, ready to welcome the one who arrives.

sens: Who has committed no fault, no sin
Who is free from moral guilt
G0361.detail:
1. The word designates one who is pure from all transgression, who has not committed sin. This is the sense that Jesus uses when he says to the accusers of the adulterous woman: "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her" (John 8:7). The expression invites everyone to recognize themselves as sinners before judging others.
2. In a broader sense, the word qualifies an absolute innocence or moral purity. It is an ideal difficult to attain for a human, as it implies the total absence of fault — which explains the silence of the accusers in the face of Jesus.
G0361.origine: The Greek word anamartētos is composed of the prefix "ana-" (indicating deprivation or negation) and "hamartētos" ("sin," related to the verb "hamartanein," "to sin," which literally means "to miss the mark"). There is also in ancient Hebrew a notion close to purity and innocence, but this Greek word creates a precise formulation of the absence of moral fault.
G0361.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 8:7, in the famous scene where Jesus defends the adulterous woman. It is used to qualify the one who would be able to throw the stone, that is, someone without sin. Jesus uses it rhetorically to show that no one is in a position to judge, as all have sinned. The context is that of moral judgment and mercy in the face of guilt.
G0361.portee: This verse teaches the believer humility in the face of judging others. Before condemning, everyone must recognize their own guilt and shortcomings. Only Jesus, completely without sin, had the right to judge — and yet he chose grace over condemnation. It is an invitation to introspection and compassion.

sens: To remain in expectation, staying in place or in suspense, in view of someone's arrival
To wait with confidence and patience for the one whose coming is hoped for
G0362.detail:
1. To wait means to remain in expectation for someone's arrival: one stays in an attitude of presence or hope, oriented towards the one who is to come. The word evokes this active pause, this time of stopping where one looks towards the future.
2. To wait also carries the nuance of confidence and patience: it is not a mere passive inaction, but a posture of assurance in the one hoped for. In 1 Thessalonians 1:10, Paul writes that believers wait for the Son of Jesus raised from the heavens: this waiting is tinged with serene certainty, for one knows that the one awaited truly returns.
G0362.origine: The Greek word is formed from the prefix "ana-" (upward, again) and "menō" (to remain, to stay). The image is that of staying in place, turned towards what is to come. The simple verb "menō" denotes the action of remaining or persevering; the prefix "ana-" adds the idea of a directed waiting, of an uplifted posture. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew "קָוָה" (qavah), which means to hope with confidence, to wait with assurance.
G0362.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 1:10. Paul describes the attitude of the churches in Thessalonica regarding the return of Christ: they wait for his resurrected Son, who has come from the heavens, to deliver them from the coming wrath. This unique occurrence in the New Testament suggests that the term is chosen for its rich connotation: it is not a mere inert waiting, but a lively expectation, marked by the confidence that the one awaited truly comes and will save.
G0362.portee: This word invites the reader to consider the believer's posture regarding the return of Christ: not anxiety or doubt, but confident and patient waiting. For the Thessalonians as for every Christian, waiting for Christ does not mean remaining idle, but staying in a living certainty that the promise will be fulfilled, and that the Son will deliver from the coming wrath. It is a hope anchored in the past resurrection and the assurance of his future coming.

sens: To bring back to mind something forgotten, to evoke memory
To bring to someone's attention an event, a word, a truth
To remember, to recall oneself, to recognize what has happened
G0363.detail:
1. To remind someone of something: it is to bring it back to their memory, as if putting back in front of their eyes what they had lost sight of. Paul tells Timothy: "I urge you to rekindle the gift of God" (2 Timothy 1:6), where the verb "urge" translates our word and literally means to bring back to mind so that he may act. It serves as a memory for someone else.
2. To strongly evoke a reality, a promise, an attitude: Paul sends Timothy to the Corinthians to "remind them of my ways in Christ" (1 Corinthians 4:17). It is not just about making them remember, but placing before their eyes again, forcefully, what should guide them.
3. To remember, when the verb is used in the passive or reflexive form: Peter "remembered" the word of Jesus after the rooster crowed (Mark 14:72), or "recalling" what had happened with the fig tree (Mark 11:21). The memory rises to the surface and strikes the heart with new power.
G0363.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb mnaomai, which means "to remember," and the prefix ana, which means "again, from above." Anamimnëskô imagines the memory descending from forgetfulness or rising to consciousness. In Hebrew, the verb zakar (to remember) expresses this action of God or man bringing to mind what matters: to remind is to "bring down the memory" from heaven so that man may act.
G0363.emploi: The verb appears six times in the New Testament, notably in Paul and in the Gospels. In Mark, it depicts moments of enlightening recognition: Peter who "remembers" and understands Jesus' warning (Mark 11:21; 14:72). Paul uses it to describe how to awaken the faith of a church: one "reminds" them of principles and examples (1 Corinthians 4:17; Hebrews 10:32). In 2 Corinthians 7:15, it is the "remembrance" of obedience that creates affection. The meaning oscillates between "to remind" (with accusative, or with the infinitive, to say what must be done) and "to remember oneself." It is a verb that awakens: it draws something from forgetfulness or drowsiness.
G0363.portee: For the reader, this verb teaches that memory is not passive: it is a living force. When Peter remembers, he weeps and repents. When the Corinthians are reminded of Paul's ways, it is to bring them back to faithfulness. It is also a call to intentionally cultivate the memory of God's words and works, for the memory that rises to consciousness produces repentance, affection, and perseverance.

sens: The action of remembering, of keeping in memory
What brings someone or something to mind
The act of commemorating, celebrating the memory of someone
A reminder, a mention intended to perpetuate the memory
G0364.detail:
1. The action of remembering, of keeping in memory: it is the act of keeping alive in the mind the memory of someone or something. It is a voluntary or deliberate act that maintains what has happened present in consciousness.
2. What brings someone or something to mind: a word, a gesture, or an action that makes someone present in the minds of those who see them. Jesus asks his disciples: "Do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19), meaning: by breaking the bread and drinking the cup, keep me present in your heart and mind.
3. The renewed or repeated memory: the periodic evocation of something. Hebrews 10:3 speaks of the "remembrance of sins" renewed each year by sacrifices, meaning that each year these rites remind the faithful of their sins and their need for forgiveness.
4. An action or word that perpetuates the memory: the act of commemoration itself, the rite that maintains the memory of someone or an event within the community.
G0364.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb that means "to remind" or "to make remember." It denotes the act opposite to forgetfulness: to bring something from a state of non-presence to consciousness into a state of presence. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates words like זָכַר (to remember) or אַזְכָּרָה (memorial) by this term, showing that in biblical thought, to remember is never purely mental: it is an action that engages the whole person and often the body (gesture, rite, word).
G0364.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in contexts of worship and communion. In Luke and Paul (1 Corinthians 11:24-25), it denotes the very reason for the Lord's Supper: the disciples must break the bread and drink the cup "in remembrance" of Jesus, that is, to keep him alive in their assembly and in their hearts. It is an act of love and fidelity towards the one who gave himself for them. In Hebrews 10:3, the word takes on a slightly different nuance: the "remembrance of sins" renewed by sacrifices expresses a troubling reality — that the rites of the Old Covenant could never definitively remove sins, only remind them year after year. Thus the word carries the idea that to remember is to make present and alive.
G0364.portee: This word teaches us that memory is not a luxury, but a spiritual necessity. When Jesus says, "Do this in remembrance of me," he invites us to intentionally maintain our relationship with him through rite and heart. The Supper is not a mere remembrance of the past, but an act that makes Jesus present among his people and binds him to his sacrifice. Conversely, Hebrews shows us that without true removal of sins, all religious commemoration remains unfinished. The Christian can therefore celebrate the Lord's table knowing that, through his death, he is not only kept in memory but freed definitively.

sens: Make new, restore what was worn or degraded
Start again, return to a state that was lost
Transform internally, remake one's way of thinking and feeling
G0365.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to make something new that has aged or worn out: it is to restore, to rejuvenate. Imagine an old garment that is made new again, or a friendship that is revived.
2. More broadly, it also means to start again, to return to a better previous state: to restore what had been lost or abandoned. The idea is one of returning to original freshness.
3. In its biblical usage in Ephesians 4:23, renewal is profoundly internal: it involves transforming the way of thinking, the heart, and the spirit. The Christian must be "renewed in the spirit of [his] mind," meaning that all his capacity to understand and judge must be made new by God's action.
G0365.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "neos" (νέος), which means "new." The prefix "ana" (ἀνα-) adds the idea of "return" or "upward movement." Thus, "ananeoomai" literally depicts the action of making anew, of rejuvenating. It is a word created to express the idea of restoration and regeneration in both the spiritual and material realms.
G0365.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 4:23. Paul uses it in the passive voice to express a transformation that the Christian must receive: this form emphasizes that renewal does not come from human effort alone, but from divine action. It is a call to allow God to deeply transform one's mind and way of seeing things. The context of Ephesians 4 deals with the change of life that must accompany conversion: it is not enough to change outwardly; a complete inner renovation of thought is necessary.
G0365.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that conversion is not just a moment, but a continuous process: God invites us to allow our understanding, thoughts, and judgments to be transformed. It is a word of freedom and hope — we are not condemned to remain trapped in our old ways of seeing; the Spirit of God can rejuvenate and regenerate the hardest heart. It is also a challenge: will we accept this profound transformation, this renovation of our mind?

sens: regain consciousness or clarity after a disturbance, dizziness, or drunkenness
be freed from an influence that disturbs the mind and regain clear judgment
G0366.detail:
1. The word literally describes the act of returning to oneself after losing consciousness or falling into drunkenness — regaining one's senses, becoming lucid again. The image is that of a person who is dazed or intoxicated finally regaining mental clarity and self-control.
2. Figuratively, it means to regain one's judgment and freedom of mind when one has been deceived or manipulated. In 2 Timothy 2:26, Paul speaks of people trapped by the devil and enslaved to his will: "returning to their senses" means that they finally break free from this influence, regain their clarity, and reclaim their own will in the face of evil's schemes.
G0366.origine: The word combines the prefix ἀνα (ana, "again, backward") with νήφω (néphō, "to be sober, to keep a clear mind"). It is the opposite of drunkenness or daze. The root νήφ- expresses the idea of mental and moral sobriety — having clear ideas, not being under the influence of a substance or foreign force. The word belongs to the family of νήφω and νήψις ("sobriety, vigilance").
G0366.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:26. Paul uses it in a context of pastoral warning: he describes men who have allowed themselves to be led into errors and carnal desires, and who have fallen under the devil's influence. "Returning to their senses" is then the means of freeing themselves from this trap and regaining a righteous life. The context shows that this "sensible judgment" is inseparable from repentance and obedience to God's will.
G0366.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the spiritual enemy seeks to disturb and enslave the mind, and that deliverance comes through regaining clarity. It invites vigilance and moral sobriety, and encourages belief that even those who have been misled can return to themselves and break free from the trap. It is a call to clarity of thought and freedom in Christ.

sens: Man from Jerusalem, husband of Sapphira, who sold a property but hid the price
Member of the young church of Jerusalem in the early days
The one who lied to the Holy Spirit and was struck dead
G0367G.detail:
1. Ananias is a man from Jerusalem who, at the beginning of the church's history, sells a property with his wife Sapphira. Contrary to what one might think, the problem is not that he does not give all the money to the apostles, but that he pretends to give the full price while withholding part of it, which amounts to lying (Acts 5:1-3).
2. As a believer in the young church, Ananias participated in the sharing of goods practiced by the early disciples after Pentecost. His act shows that even among those who followed Jesus, there was room for dishonesty and hypocrisy.
3. When Peter rebukes him for allowing Satan to fill his heart and for lying to the Holy Spirit, Ananias falls dead (Acts 5:5). This immediate judgment illustrates God's holiness and the seriousness with which the Holy Spirit regards lying and hypocrisy in the church.
G0367G.origine: The name Ananias comes from the Hebrew Hananiah (חֲנַנְיָה), which means "God has been gracious" or "the Lord has been gracious." It is a name carrying a divine promise. It is borne by several people in the Bible, but this one is particularly known for the dramatic event in Acts where his lie to the apostles costs him his life.
G0367G.emploi: The name Ananias in Acts refers to three different men depending on the historical context and references: the one from Jerusalem (Acts 5:1-5) who sells a property with his wife, a believer from Damascus (mentioned in Acts 9 and 22) who helps Paul after his conversion, and a high priest (Acts 23-24) who presides over the Sanhedrin. The provided usages concern only the first: the man from Jerusalem in the early days of the apostolic church. His story is brief but intense: it shows how lying and hypocrisy do not remain hidden before God and how the young community took the presence of the Holy Spirit seriously.
G0367G.portee: The story of Ananias reminds us that God judges the heart and not the appearance, and that honesty toward God and the church is a fruit of the Holy Spirit dwelling in us. His immediate punishment is not a lesson in harshness, but a warning: the Christian life requires total sincerity. It invites us to examine our own intentions when we approach God and His people.

sens: Disciple of Damascus who restored sight to Saul of Tarsus
Pious man respected by the Jews of Damascus
G0367H.detail:
1. Ananias is a disciple of Jesus living in Damascus at the time of the Apostle Paul. The Lord appears to him in a vision and sends him to Saul (who becomes Paul) to lay hands on him so that he may regain his sight after his experience on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:10-17). It is through Ananias that God accomplishes the healing and filling of the Holy Spirit for the future apostle to the Gentiles.
2. Ananias is described as a pious man who observes the Jewish law and enjoys an excellent reputation among all the Jews of Damascus (Acts 22:12). He is a respected believer in his community, which makes his humble obedience to the Lord's vision regarding Saul, his persecutor, all the more remarkable.
G0367H.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew 'Hananyas (חֲנַנְיָה), which means "Yahweh has been gracious" or "the Lord has been merciful." It is composed of 'Hanan (grace) and Yah (Yahweh). This name was common in Israel and carries a promise of divine mercy.
G0367H.emploi: Ananias of Damascus appears in Acts chapters 9 and 22, where he plays a decisive role in the conversion and mission of Paul. When Saul arrives in Damascus as a persecutor of Christians, the Lord reveals Himself to him on the road and sends him to Damascus. It is Ananias whom the Lord chooses to welcome the new apostle, lay hands on him, and fill him with the Holy Spirit (Acts 9:10-17). Paul himself, testifying before the Sanhedrin, recalls this encounter and praises Ananias's piety (Acts 22:12). It is a remarkable example of faithfulness and obedience to the voice of God, even in the face of a task that seems contrary to appearances.
G0367H.portee: Ananias teaches the Christian the importance of immediate obedience to God, even when His will seems strange or dangerous. Ananias fears Saul (Acts 9:13), knows him as a persecutor, and yet he obeys; it is through this that God accomplishes the miracle of Paul's conversion. His name, which evokes the grace of God, reminds us that the Lord acts with mercy and calls His children to participate in His works, even the most unexpected ones.

sens: High priest at the time of the Apostle Paul
G0367I.detail: 1. Ananias is a Jewish high priest who exercises his authority in Jerusalem at the time of Paul's trial. He presides over the Sanhedrin (the Jewish court) and orders Paul to be struck on the mouth during his interrogation (Acts 23:2), showing his hostility toward the apostle. A few days later, he himself appears before the Roman governor Felix to accuse Paul, accompanied by elders and the orator Tertullus (Acts 24:1).
G0367I.origine: The name Ananias comes from the Hebrew Hanania, which means "the Lord has been gracious" or "grace of God." It is a name borne by several characters in the Old Testament (notably a prophet during Jeremiah's time). Three different men bear this name in the New Testament: the believer from Jerusalem who dies for lying to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5), the disciple from Damascus who helps Paul (Acts 9), and this high priest who pursues him in court.
G0367I.emploi: Ananias the high priest appears twice in the Acts of the Apostles, both times during Paul's trial in Jerusalem and Caesarea (around 50-58 A.D.). He embodies the opposition of official Judaism to apostolic preaching. The historian Josephus also mentions him: he is a known historical figure, a Sadducean high priest who will play a role in the events leading to the Jewish revolt against Rome.
G0367I.portee: The mention of Ananias reminds the reader that the persecution of the Church did not come only from pagan Rome, but also from the Jewish religious establishment. It shows how Paul, once a persecutor himself, becomes in turn a victim of official persecution. This episode illustrates the growing opposition between the synagogue and the early Church.

sens: That cannot be contradicted or denied
That imposes itself as true and does not allow for discussion
That is so evident that it cannot be refuted
G0368.detail:
1. The word designates what cannot be contradicted: it cannot be fought against with arguments or denied. It is something so manifest that contradiction becomes impossible. In Acts 19:36, the angry crowd in Ephesus is urged to recognize that the facts are undeniable: the greatness of the goddess Artemis and the role of the city are not in question.
2. By extension, it is what imposes itself as an unavoidable, indisputable truth. No argument can refute it, and no one can reasonably contest it. It is a fact or a reality that must be accepted as is.
3. The term can also qualify what is clearly established, recognized as certain by all. It is something that no one, in all reason, can refute or doubt.
