G0368.origine: The word is composed of three Greek elements: "an-" (not), "anti-" (against), and "rētos" (said, spoken, stated). Literally, it is what cannot be said against or contradicted. It comes from the same root as "rhêma" (word) and "légô" (to say). The basic idea is that of a word or reality that no opposing word or discourse can destroy or contradict.
G0368.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 19:36. It is found in a context of urban turmoil: an agitated crowd in Ephesus threatens to cause disorder over the worship of Artemis. The town clerk calms the crowd by telling them that certain facts (the glory of Ephesus, the worship of the goddess) are "undeniable" and that therefore there is no need to get excited or act hastily. The word serves to call for calm based on realities that cannot be denied.
G0368.portee: This word reminds us that some truths impose themselves and that it is futile to fight against them. In the biblical context, it is a call to wisdom: recognizing what is manifest and evident allows for better decision-making and avoids sterile agitation. For the believer, it invites discernment between what is established and what is debatable.

sens: Without opposition or resistance
Without contesting or discussing
Without hesitation or refusal
G0369.detail:
1. Without opposition or resistance: the word describes one who does not oppose, who raises no obstacle. Peter tells Cornelius that he has come "without objection" (Acts 10:29), meaning without rejecting the invitation, without an argument to refuse.
2. Without contesting or discussing: it is acting without doubt, without questioning. When one does something "without objection," one does not discuss the reasons, one simply accepts.
3. Without hesitation or refusal: the adverb expresses the idea of a free and complete acceptance, without ulterior motives or reluctance regarding what is asked.
G0369.origine: The Greek word is composed of three elements: "an-" (negation, "without"), "anti-" ("against", "in front of"), and "rhētōs" ("spoken", "stated"). The basic image is that of a word raised against something — an objection, a verbal contradiction. By placing the negation "an-" in front, we obtain the opposite: a word that does not oppose, a tranquil acceptance. It is a rare word, coined to express this idea of unreserved consent.
G0369.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 10:29. Peter responds to Cornelius by explaining that he has come "without objection" after receiving a divine vision commanding him not to refuse to meet with Gentiles. The context shows that this acceptance "without objection" is precisely the result of Peter's obedience to God's revelation: he did not argue, did not hesitate, he simply obeyed and came. It is a key moment where Peter crosses a major religious barrier without resistance, because God commanded him to do so.
G0369.portee: This word speaks to us of unreserved obedience and consent freed from our doubts. When Peter comes "without objection," he shows what it means to accept God's will even when it disrupts our habits and certainties. For us, it invites us to examine our own objections — our hesitations, our inner resistances — and to seek whether they come from God or from our fears.

sens: Who does not deserve something
Who is not up to a task or responsibility
Who lacks moral or spiritual value to accomplish something
G0370.detail:
1. The word describes a person who does not have the required qualities to receive or do something — they are simply not worthy of it. It conveys the idea of not being "up to par".
2. It is particularly strong when speaking of a responsibility or judgment: to be unworthy is to lack the moral or spiritual competence to assume it. In 1 Corinthians 6:2, Paul ironically asks the Corinthians if they consider themselves unworthy to render even the most ordinary judgments — which would be absurd for those who will one day judge the world.
3. The word also carries the idea of spiritual unworthiness: one does not have the stature, honor, or moral purity that one should have for this charge.
G0370.origine: The word is formed from the privative prefix "an-" (which means "not") and the term "axios" (worthy, valuable). The root suggests the idea of weighing, evaluating — worthy is what "weighs" enough to deserve something. Unworthy is simply its negation: what does not weigh enough, what is not valuable.
G0370.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 6:2. Paul uses it rhetorically: he ironically asks the believers in Corinth if they are unworthy to judge small matters — in reality, they should be quite worthy of doing so, since one day they will judge the world with Christ. The irony dramatizes the contrast: how could people called to a cosmic judgment be unworthy to arbitrate earthly disputes? It is a veiled exhortation to rise to the level of their calling.
G0370.portee: This word challenges the believer regarding their dignity in Christ. Paul does not say that the Corinthians are objectively unworthy; he provokes them to recognize that they have received in Christ such a great calling that no earthly task should find them failing. It is a call to live up to what they have become by grace — worthy, because they belong to Christ.

sens: In an unworthy manner, without the respect or piety that one should have
With an attitude that is not suitable for the holiness or importance of what one is doing
G0371.detail:
1. The word speaks to the manner in which something is done: indignantly, that is, without the respect and seriousness that one should show. When Paul says that one must not eat the Lord's bread "unworthily" (1 Corinthians 11:27), he means that eating and drinking at the Lord's Supper lightly, without considering what one is doing, without recognizing the importance and holiness of the body and blood of Christ, is a serious lack of respect towards God.
2. It is an attitude that does not correspond to what one should be in the face of something holy. One who communes unworthily, without preparing their heart, without asking if their life aligns with the Gospel, acts against what the Supper demands and will be "guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 11:29).
G0371.origine: The word comes from the verb "ἄξιος" (axiōs) which means "worthy, valuable." By adding the prefix "ἀν-" (an-) which means "not" or "no," we get "not worthy": unworthy. This formation clearly shows the idea: it is not being up to the importance of this moment or object. It is the opposite of the word "worthily" (ἀξίως).
G0371.emploi: Paul uses this word only once in the New Testament, but in a crucial passage about the Supper. In 1 Corinthians 11:27-29, the apostle warns the Corinthians that eating and drinking unworthily, that is, without respecting the deep meaning of this communion in the body and blood of Christ, exposes one to God's judgment. The divided Corinthians, who were fighting and despising each other during the Lord's meal, were committing precisely this fault: they were profaning a holy act by lacking respect and brotherly love.
G0371.portee: This word reminds the believer that communion at the Lord's table is not an ordinary gesture, but an act that engages their whole person. One must come with respect, after examining their heart and their relationship with God and others. It teaches us that our worship and acts of devotion reflect what we truly think of God: doing things lightly shows that we do not take God seriously.

sens: The cessation of work or physical effort
The calming of the soul, inner peace
The absence of agitation or torment
The cessation of an action (refrain, interruption)
G0372.detail: 1. Rest is primarily the cessation of work and physical fatigue: it is what a wandering spirit seeks in the desert when it wants to find a place to rest (Matthew 12:43, Luke 11:24). 2. It is also and especially an inner peace of the soul, a calming of the heart that Jesus offers to those who come to him with their burdens: "You will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:29). It is less the absence of work than the tranquility and lightness of heart. 3. Rest also means the absence of continuous torment: the cursed who worship the beast have "no rest day or night" (Revelation 14:11), which underscores the intensity of their endless suffering. 4. In some contexts, the word takes on the meaning of "ceasing," of interrupting a repeated action: living beings do not cease to sing day and night (Revelation 4:8), meaning they have no interruption.
G0372.origine: The word comes from the verb anapauô (ἀναπαύω), composed of ana ("again") and pausô ("stop, cease"). The starting image is that of rest returning, of a desirable interruption that revitalizes. In Greek, the word aneasis (ἄνεσις), a cousin, evokes rather relaxation as the release of previous tension. In the Greek Old Testament, anapausis primarily translates the Hebrew word "nuah," which means "to rest" or "to dwell quietly," and also "shabbat," the sacred day of rest.
G0372.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospels and Revelation. In Matthew and Luke, it refers to the rest sought by the unclean spirit without a fixed dwelling, and also the rest of the soul that Christ promises to his weary disciples. In Revelation, the meaning fades or reverses: the heavenly beings "never cease" singing (4:8), while the cursed are deprived of all rest (14:11). It is a rather rare word, which emphasizes not sleep but peace or interruption.
G0372.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize that Jesus offers much more than a pause: a true rest for the soul, a lasting peace for those who place their burdens in His hands. It also reminds us that the promised rest is not passive or eternal in this world; it frees us to serve with a lightened heart and a clear conscience.

sens: Cease work, fatigue, or activity to regain strength
Experience relief, inner peace after tension or worry
Relax in inactivity, enjoy calm and well-being
Leave something at rest, without agitation
G0373.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to cease physical work to regain strength. Jesus invites his weary disciples: "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while" (Mark 6:31). It is the necessary interruption after effort.
2. The word also denotes emotional or spiritual rest, an inner calming. Jesus promises: "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28) — it is the relief from the pain and burden that the soul carries.
3. Sometimes the word simply evokes a state of relaxation, serene inactivity: the soul of the rich man in the parable says, "Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry" (Luke 12:19), seeking well-being without worry.
4. The word can also mean to bring tranquility to someone else, to refresh a troubled mind. Paul asks Philemon: "Refresh my heart in Christ" (Philemon 1:20), meaning remove my anxiety and make me serene.
G0373.origine: The Greek word is composed of "ana" ("again", "back") and "pauo" ("cease", "stop"). The starting image is that of a stop, a cessation — one ceases work to return to a normal state. The Hebrew word from the Old Testament that the Greek most often translates is "nuakh", which literally means "to settle", "to rest": like a dove that finally lands after flying. This root also appears in words of the same Greek family meaning "rest" or "place of rest."
G0373.emploi: The verb appears twelve times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and in Paul's letters. Its usage varies according to context: in the Gospels, it denotes the physical rest of the disciples (Mark 6:31, Mark 14:41) or the spiritual rest that Jesus offers to those who suffer (Matthew 11:28). In Paul's letters, it often takes on an emotional or relational hue: bringing peace of mind to someone (Philemon 1:20, 2 Corinthians 7:13). In Revelation, it evokes eschatological rest, the rest that awaits the martyrs in the afterlife (Revelation 6:11, Revelation 14:13). The word can be active ("give rest") or passive/reflexive ("rest", "be comforted").
G0373.portee: This word teaches the reader that rest is not a luxury or laziness, but a need and a right before God. Jesus himself invites to rest, showing that the life of faith is not an endless exhaustion. The spiritual rest that Jesus offers — liberation from the burden of sin and anxiety — is the heart of the Gospel. For the believer, this word also speaks of the promise of eternal peace to come, and the importance of comforting and supporting the hearts of others in faith.

sens: Encourage someone to act or believe something
Incite to an action or belief deemed wrong or unacceptable
G0374.detail:
1. The verb means to push or incite someone to do something. It is a call to action that comes from outside, a strong persuasion. In Acts 18:13, the Jews accuse Paul of stirring up — pushing — people to serve God in a way that contravenes Jewish law.
2. When the context specifies, it incites to something bad or forbidden. The word then carries a negative nuance: it is not a simple invitation, but an incitement to transgress or rebel. In Acts 18:13, this negative sense is clear: the accusers reproach Paul for turning people away from respecting the law.
G0374.origine: The word comes from the prefix ana- ("again", "up") and peithō ("persuade", "convince"). Together, it reinforces the idea: to persuade vigorously, to incite strongly. In Hebrew, Jeremiah 29:8 expresses a similar idea with a verb meaning "to lift" or "to carry": to lift someone to action is to push them to act.
G0374.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament in Acts 18:13, in an accusation brought against Paul before the Roman magistrate Gallio in Corinth. The local Jews denounce Paul by claiming that he stirs people to worship God "contrary to the law." This context shows how the verb describes a persuasion perceived as dangerous or subversive: Paul does not merely preach, he actively urges his listeners to change their religious practice, which offends the Jewish authorities.
G0374.portee: This word reminds us of the power of speech to transform convictions and actions. Paul is accused not only of believing differently but of inciting others to believe. For the Christian, this raises a question: how to share one's faith without imposing, how to convince without manipulating? The text also shows that the proclamation of the Gospel will sometimes be perceived as a threat by those who defend the established order.

sens: Send upwards, to a higher authority
Send someone to another person or place
Return something or someone to its owner
G0375.detail:
1. Send someone to a higher or more important authority. Jesus is "sent back" to Herod by Pilate (Luke 23:7), because Herod has power over Galilee; then Herod "sends him back" to Pilate (Luke 23:11). It is passing the case to a superior.
2. Return someone to someone else, or escort them back to their original destination. Paul requests to be "sent back" to Caesar to be judged in Rome according to his appeal (Acts 25:21); Herod, having examined Jesus, "sends him back" to Pilate without finding anything to condemn him (Luke 23:15).
3. Return someone or something to the one who entrusted it. Philemon asks Paul: "I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart" (Philemon 1:12) — it is about Onesimus, the runaway slave, whom Paul returns to his master with a request for forgiveness and reconciliation.
G0375.origine: The word comes from the prefix "ana-" (again, back) and "pempō" (send). The basic image is that of sending someone again, either upwards (in ancient Greece, authors use it to send to a god or authority), or in the opposite direction. The composition suggests a movement of return or redirection.
G0375.emploi: This verb appears five times in the New Testament, concentrated in three passages. Three occurrences are found in the Passion narrative of Luke (23:7, 11, 15), where Pilate and Herod "send back" Jesus to each other — each refusing to judge him and passing him to the other authority. One occurrence is in Acts 25:21, where Paul mentions that his case must be "sent back" to the Roman emperor, showing the application of the word to a judicial transfer to a higher authority. Finally, Philemon 1:12 uses it in a very human context: Paul "sends back" to Philemon his slave Onesimus, once a runaway, now converted — it is an act of reconciliation and trust.
G0375.portee: This word reveals how human justice passes from hand to hand, and how it is subject to power plays: Jesus is tossed between Pilate and Herod. But it also shows that true authority — that of the Father — never "sends back"; it judges with justice. For the reader, Philemon 1:12 teaches authentic reconciliation: Onesimus is not sent back as a mere package, but as a beloved brother, which completely transforms the meaning of the gesture.

sens: Who has one or more disabled or mutilated limbs
Who cannot use their arms or legs normally
(Figuratively) Who lacks the necessary ability or strength
G0376.detail:
1. The word describes a person whose body is damaged or mutilated, particularly in the arms or legs. In Luke 14:13 and 14:21, Jesus refers to those who are "crippled" to describe severely disabled individuals who are unable to work or move normally.
2. It refers to someone whose limbs do not function properly: they may be missing a hand, an arm, a leg, or have them so damaged that they can no longer be used. These individuals cannot therefore provide for their own needs.
3. In a figurative context, the word can evoke any incapacity or powerlessness, although this meaning is not attested in the New Testament.
G0376.origine: The Greek word comes from "ana-" (upward movement) and "peros" (mutilated, damaged). The image is that of a mutilation or injury that has deformed or removed a part of the body. It is a compound word that emphasizes the idea of a profound alteration of the normal shape of the body.
G0376.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Gospel of Luke (14:13 and 14:21). Both occurrences are found in the same parable: that of the master who invites not his rich friends to his feast, but the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind. Jesus uses this term to evoke the extreme misery of certain people of his time, unable to return the invitation or offer anything in return. The accumulation of these terms (poor, crippled, lame, blind) paints a picture of the greatest poverty and absolute need.
G0376.portee: This word from Jesus invites believers to direct their generosity not toward those who can return something to us, but toward the weakest and most destitute. The crippled, in biblical language, represents one who cannot give anything in return: it is a call to the gratuitousness of Christian love. It serves as a warning against seeking recognition or profit in the help we provide to others.

sens: To sit or lie down to have a meal
To recline or lean back at the table
To take a place at the table, particularly in a position of honor
G0377.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to sit or lie down to eat a meal, as one does with family or on a special occasion. It is an action that marks the beginning of sharing a meal. When Jesus feeds the crowd on the mountain, he has the crowd "sit down on the ground" (Matthew 15:35) before breaking the bread.

2. In more formal meals, particularly at a host's table, the word describes the particular position of the guest — often reclining or leaning on an elbow, according to the customs of the time. This is the posture Jesus takes when he "sat at the table" at the Pharisee's house (Luke 11:37) or during the Last Supper (Luke 22:14). John describes Jesus "leaning" on the breast of the beloved disciple at the table (John 13:25).

3. The word is also used to describe one who takes a place at the table, particularly in a position of honor or importance. When Jesus tells his guest to go "sit in the lowest place" to be exalted (Luke 14:10), he is speaking of the position one occupies at the table, a sign of the respect afforded to them.
G0377.origine: The Greek word comes from "ana" (upward, backward) and "piptô" (to fall, to stretch out). The basic image is that of leaning back — hence the classical meaning "to fall backward." But in the later usage of Greek, the word has shifted toward the idea of stretching out or sitting down to eat, particularly in a reclining or supported position, as was customary at the table among the Greeks and Romans. It is a sibling word to the verbs "anaklínô" (to make recline at the table) and "anákeimai" (to be reclining at the table).
G0377.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Gospel, exclusively in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. It describes two main contexts: first, the crowd sitting on the ground to eat (Matthew 15:35; Mark 6:40, 8:6; John 6:10), a simple and ordinary situation. Secondly, meals at the table, particularly at a host's house or on solemn occasions — Jesus at the Pharisee's house (Luke 11:37), at a banquet (Luke 14:10, 22:14), at the Last Supper (John 13:12, 13:25, 21:20), where the word emphasizes the secluded position and intimacy of the moment. The meaning does not vary much: it is always the action of taking a position to eat.
G0377.portee: This ordinary word reminds us that Jesus shared meals with people — crowds on the mountain, tax collectors at the table, apostles at the Supper. These moments of eating together mark welcome, communion, and teaching. For the reader, it is an invitation to see the meal as an act of grace and a fraternal bond that God Himself honors.

sens: To completely fill, to make full
To realize, to bring to completion what was expected
To supply what is lacking, to fill an absence
To fully observe a law or commandment
G0378.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to fill a space or container to the brim: to make something complete and whole. This is why Stephanas and his companions "supply your absence" (1 Corinthians 16:17) by holding your place through their presence and service.

2. To fulfill means to bring to completion what was promised or predicted: the prophecy of Isaiah "is fulfilled" in that people refuse to understand and see (Matthew 13:14). The expectation becomes reality.

3. To supply means to provide what was lacking so that something is whole: Epaphroditus risked his life "to supply your absence" in service to Paul (Philippians 2:30). He filled the void left by the absence of the Philippians.

4. To observe a law means to practice it fully, to make it a living reality: "You will thus fulfill the law of Christ" by bearing one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2). It is to fill the law with its true meaning.
G0378.origine: The word is composed of ἀνα ("upward, again") and πληρόω ("to fill, to complete"). The latter root comes from the ancient Greek πλήρης, "full." In Hebrew, the verb מָלֵא (malé, to fill) and שָׁלַם (shalam, to complete, to perfect) carry the image: to fulfill is to make something full, whole, complete. The preposition ἀνα adds the idea of starting again, of bringing to completion what had been interrupted.
G0378.emploi: This verb appears 6 times in the New Testament at the provided locations. It serves to express three contexts: 1) the fulfillment of prophecies (Matthew 13:14), where it shows that the word of God is realized concretely; 2) the filling of a place or absence (1 Corinthians 14:16, 16:17, Philippians 2:30), where it describes how someone fills a void left by another; 3) the observance of a law or commandment (Galatians 6:2), where it expresses faithful practice. In 1 Thessalonians 2:16, the meaning is more bitter: the Jews "fill up their sins," meaning they accumulate them to the point of saturation, until the measure is full and judgment falls.
G0378.portee: This word teaches Christians that God leaves nothing unresolved: His promises are fulfilled, His laws demand complete and joyful obedience. It also reminds us that each believer has a role to play in supplying the weaknesses or absences of others, so that the assembly is complete and the service of Christ continues. It is a lesson in commitment and fraternal solidarity.

sens: Who cannot justify or excuse themselves
Who has no valid excuse
Whose actions or judgments cannot be defended
G0379.detail:
1. The word designates one who cannot present any excuse before a judge. It is a legal term: one is "inexcusable" when there is nothing to say in their defense. In Romans 1:20, Paul states that humans are without excuse because God has clearly revealed Himself in creation: they have seen enough evidence to believe, thus no excuse is acceptable.
2. More broadly, being inexcusable means being defenseless before judgment. One who judges others while committing the same faults cannot excuse themselves: they condemn themselves by their own law (Romans 2:1). Their double standard has no justification.
G0379.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: the particle "an-" (negation) and "apologeisthai" (to defend oneself, to justify). It literally depicts someone from whom all possibility of "apology" is removed, that is, a plea in their favor. In classical Greek, it was primarily a judicial term: the inexcusable accused could not invoke any mitigating circumstances. The Bible uses it to express the impossibility of escaping divine judgment.
G0379.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in two verses of Romans. In 1:20, it qualifies humans who reject God despite the evident proofs of His existence in nature: their excuses (ignorance, doubt) do not hold. In 2:1, it applies to the critic who practices the same sins they condemn: they are doubly inexcusable, for no one is fooled by this hypocrisy. In both cases, Paul wants to show that there is no flaw in God's judgment — all resistance to divine truth is indefensible.
G0379.portee: This word reminds the reader that before God, no excuse exists for rejecting His call. Whether through supposed ignorance of His creation (1:20) or moral hypocrisy (2:1), conscience and facts render everyone inexcusable. It is a call to sincerity with oneself: one cannot indefinitely hide what they know to be true. For the Christian, this invites transparency in judgment of others and recognition of one's own faults rather than justifying them.

sens: To open by unrolling a rolled manuscript
To unfold, to deploy an object rolled upon itself
G0380.detail: 1. To open a scroll of parchment or papyrus rolled up by gradually unrolling it to read its content. This is the action Jesus performs in the synagogue of Nazareth when handed the scroll of Isaiah: He unrolls it to find the passage He wants to read (Luke 4:17). In biblical times, sacred texts were not bound in codex (stitched booklets), but preserved on scrolls that had to be unrolled with one hand while rolling up the other to advance in reading. 2. More broadly, to deploy or extend a rolled object. The verb describes the concrete physical gesture of undoing what is rolled to make it accessible or visible.
G0380.origine: The Greek verb ἀναπτύσσω is formed from the prefix ἀνα- ("upward, again") and the verb πτύσσω ("to roll, to fold"). The image is that of unrolling what was rolled, that is, opening by a movement opposite to that which rolls. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the word פָּרַשׂ (parash, "to extend, to unfold") expresses a similar idea.
G0380.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:17, in the scene where Jesus attends the synagogue service in Nazareth and unrolls the scroll of the prophet Isaiah to read a messianic passage. This unique occurrence shows the common Jewish practice: every public reader of the Torah or the Prophets had to handle the scrolls in this manner. The act of unrolling was a mundane yet essential act to access the sacred text.
G0380.portee: This word brings us back to the tangible reality of Jewish religious life in the first century and the respect with which sacred texts were handled. By seeing Jesus Himself unroll the scroll of Isaiah, we understand that even the Son of God participated in the ordinary practices of the synagogue. This simple gesture also emphasizes the importance of actively seeking the Word of God: it is not enough for the scroll to be present; it must be unrolled to be read and understood.

sens: To set fire to something, to ignite it
To make something burn, to produce a flame
To excite, provoke, trigger (in a figurative sense)
G0381.detail:
1. The word primarily means to set fire to an object, to ignite it: Jesus in Luke 12:49 speaks of a fire He has come to cast upon the earth that is already "kindled," meaning actively burning.

2. It designates the action of making something burn or producing a flame that consumes: the tongue is compared to a small fire that can "kindle" a great forest in James 3:5, showing the destructive power of a small ignited thing.

3. Figuratively, the word evokes the idea of triggering, provoking a chain reaction, like a fire that spreads: it is this image of propagation and inflammation that serves to describe how words can cause great damage.
G0381.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to attach" or "to fix," but with the prefix "ana" (upward, back) it takes on the meaning of "to set on fire." It is a compound verb: the initial particle reinforces the idea of a flame that rises and develops. The word evokes the concrete action of igniting wood or fuel.
G0381.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament Greek. In Luke 12:49, Jesus uses it to speak of the spiritual fire He brings to the world that begins to manifest. In James 3:5, the apostle uses it in his description of the havoc caused by the tongue: a small flame can kindle a great forest, a powerful image of the destructive power of speech. In both cases, the verb describes an action that begins and amplifies, a fire that spreads.
G0381.portee: This word reminds us of the explosive force of words and spiritual influences. For Jesus, the fire speaks of judgment and purification that has already begun. For James, it warns us that our words, even seemingly light, can cause considerable damage around us. It is a call to monitor our speech and understand the real gravity of what we say.

sens: That cannot be counted, too numerous to be numbered
That exceeds so much in quantity that one gives up counting
Immense, incalculable in size
G0382.detail:
1. The word first describes what is materially impossible or impractical to count: too many things, too many elements. In Hebrews 11:12, Paul speaks of Abraham's offspring, so numerous "as the stars of heaven, as the sand by the seashore that cannot be counted" — the classic image from the Old Testament to express the impossibility of enumeration.
2. The meaning extends to what is simply so great, so vast, that no number accounts for it. It is less a question of technique (could I count long enough?) than an affirmation: it exceeds all calculation, all human measure.
G0382.origine: The word is formed from the privative prefix "an-" (which means "not," "without") and the root "arithm-" (from the verb "arithméô," to count). It literally means "without number." This simple construction speaks volumes: the absence of number signifies the absence of limit, the profusion. In Hebrews 11:12, Paul takes up the biblical image of Abraham whose descendants cannot be counted — a promise of God that is fulfilled infinitely.
G0382.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:12, to qualify Abraham's offspring. It is the key moment where the author of Hebrews celebrates Abraham's faith: despite his aged body, he believed God's promise of an innumerable offspring. The context is not a simple enumeration, but an act of faith that materializes in the impossible, in the surpassing of all human calculation. This uniqueness of the word makes it a strong, solemn expression, suited to the grandeur of the promise.
G0382.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the nature of God's promise: it is neither stingy nor measured. Abraham, old and without strength, receives the certainty of an offspring that escapes all enumeration — a sign that God's faithfulness infinitely surpasses human capacities and wisdom. For the believer, "innumerable" reminds us that God's grace knows no limits, and that His blessing is counted in terms of abundance, not restriction.

sens: Agitate, shake physically
Raise, put into motion
Incite a crowd to action
Push someone to revolt or hostility
G0383.detail:
1. In its primary physical sense, the word means to agitate or shake something — to move it from side to side. This is the basic image of the Greek word.
2. From this comes a more figurative sense: to raise, to put into motion in the sense of shaking or moving emotionally. It transitions from the physical to the psychological.
3. The word is used to excite a crowd, to push it to action. In Mark 15:11, the chief priests "excite" the crowd against Jesus, meaning they manipulate and animate it against him so that it demands the release of Barabbas.
4. It can also mean to stir up the people, to incite them to revolt or hostility. In Luke 23:5, Jesus' accusers declare that he "stirs up" the people by pushing them to revolt through his teaching.
G0383.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἀνα- ("upward, again") and the verb σείω ("shake, agitate"). The starting image is therefore that of shaking upward or making something move. It is a classical verb in ancient Greek. Its meaning has extended, especially in late texts, from the physical domain (shaking an object) to the psychological and social domain (exciting emotions or collective action).
G0383.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, both in the Passion narratives according to Mark and Luke. In Mark 15:11, it describes how the religious leaders actively manipulate the crowd to demand Barabbas instead of Jesus. In Luke 23:5, it is used to accuse Jesus of having stirred up the people, inciting them to revolt through his itinerant teaching. In both cases, the word carries a negative connotation: it refers to malicious agitation, a deliberate action intended to create trouble and hostility. The Gospels show how this verb was used against Jesus during his trial.
G0383.portee: This word reveals how Jesus was portrayed by his adversaries as a dangerous agitator, a disruptor of order. It also shows the power of religious leaders to manipulate and stir up a crowd. For the Christian, it serves as a reminder that Jesus was persecuted by a coordinated power system; but also a warning against the danger of allowing collective emotions to dominate us without discernment. The word emphasizes how the truth of Jesus has disturbed and continues to disturb.

sens: Disturb, deeply trouble someone in their moral or spiritual stability
Undermine someone's confidence or conviction through words or ideas
G0384.detail:
1. The verb depicts the action of shaking, disturbing someone to their very core. It is like putting into disorder the convictions or inner peace that someone possessed. In Acts 15:24, men "disturbed" the souls of the believers in Jerusalem by holding troubling speeches about the Law: they sowed doubt and anxiety among Christians who were previously serene in their faith.
2. The word also suggests destabilization through cunning words or false ideas. It is not a mere inconvenience, but an attack on the very solidity of what one believes or experiences. This is why the apostle Paul and the other leaders in Jerusalem consider these men as having troubled the Church with false claims.
G0384.origine: The word comes from a very concrete image: literally, "to pack and remove," from the Greek word σκεῦος (skeuos), which designates an object, a utensil, a load. From there, it has extended to the idea of "undoing," "dismantling," "devastating." Applied to souls or spirits, it retains this force: to disturb deeply, as one would disrupt or plunder a village by removing all its goods. It is a rare verb in the New Testament, which underscores the importance of the moment it is used.
G0384.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 15:24, in the context of the Jerusalem council. Men came from Jerusalem without apostolic mandate preaching that Christians from paganism must follow the Law of Moses. The apostle Peter and the other apostles, in writing to the churches in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia, denounce these men as having "disturbed" the souls of the believers by their words. The word powerfully expresses the spiritual damage that false teachings can inflict: not a mere temporary confusion, but a real emotional and doctrinal shock.
G0384.portee: This word reminds today's Christians of the real power of human teachings and seductive speeches to disturb faith. It invites us to remain firm in the Gospel we have received directly from Christ and the apostles, without being shaken by added doctrines or human traditions presented as mandatory. It also highlights the early Church's concern to protect its members from these disturbances.

sens: Pull towards oneself or upwards with effort
Remove, take away from a situation or place
Make disappear, cause to cease
G0385.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to pull upwards": it is the physical action of extracting something by pulling. In Luke 14:5, Jesus asks his interlocutors: "Which of you, if his son or his ox falls into a well, will not immediately pull him out on the Sabbath?" — it is indeed the concrete gesture of pulling the animal out of the well to save it.
2. In the same context, the word more broadly denotes the action of removing something from where it is: getting someone or something out of danger or prison.
3. In Acts 11:10, the sheet filled with all kinds of animals is "taken up" to heaven: the image becomes more abstract, simply meaning that the sheet disappears, is removed from Peter's field of vision.
G0385.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "ana" (upward, again) and the verb "spáō" (to pull, to tear away). The starting image is one of energetic pulling, of tearing away. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words like "lāqach" (to take) and "ālāh" (to ascend), conveying the idea of pulling something upwards or removing it.
G0385.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 14:5, it describes the act of rescuing an animal that has fallen into a well — Jesus uses it to show that doing good to a creature takes precedence over strict observance of the Sabbath. In Acts 11:10, it refers to the removal of the sheet from Peter's vision during his mysterious vision. The meaning is always that of an energetic action that removes or extracts something from a given position.
G0385.portee: This word sheds light on Jesus' teaching about concrete mercy: saving a life, even on the Sabbath, is a good and natural act. For the Christian, it reminds us that active love takes precedence over rules, and that true piety is manifested by the help offered to those who suffer.

sens: action of rising up, getting up
return to life of a deceased person
general resurrection of all the dead at the end of time
resurrection of Christ in particular
resurrection to eternal life or to judgment
G0386.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the physical action of rising up or getting up. In Luke 2:34, the child Jesus is presented as one who will bring about the "rising" of many in Israel — an idea of restoration and recovery.

2. It then signifies the return to life of a deceased person. Hebrews 11:35 mentions righteous individuals from the Old Testament who were raised to life individually, such as the prophet Elijah who brought the widow's son back to life.

3. The general resurrection of the dead is a major theme in the Gospels and Acts: all the dead will rise at the end of time (Matthew 22:23-31; Acts 24:15). The Sadducees, who denied this doctrine, contested it with Jesus.

4. The resurrection of Christ holds a central place: Acts 4:33 reports that the apostles testified "with great power" to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and 1 Corinthians 15:21 states that "by a man came the resurrection of the dead."

5. John 5:29 distinguishes two resurrections: one "to life" (paradise) and one "to judgment" (condemnation). There are not one, but two resurrections according to each person's destiny.
G0386.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "anistemi" (to rise, to stand up) preceded by the prefix "ana" (upward, back). The basic image is thus a movement upward, a restoration. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it often renders the Hebrew word "qum" (to rise, to stand), which highlights its concrete meaning. It is a very expressive compound word: ana (to rise) + stasis (position, station), thus literally "to be put back in a standing position," hence "rising" or "resurrection."
G0386.emploi: The word appears about 40 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul, in the Gospels, and in Acts. It encompasses three main usages. First, a concrete and rare sense: the physical rising of a person (Luke 2:34). Next, the resurrection of Christ, the heart of apostolic faith: the apostles constantly testify to it (Acts 1:22; 2:31; 4:33; Romans 1:4; 1 Peter 1:3). Finally, and most importantly, the general resurrection of the dead is the major subject of debate between Jesus and the Sadducees (Matthew 22:23-31; Mark 12:18-23; Luke 20:27-36), who denied it, while the Pharisees and Christians affirm it. Paul elaborates extensively on this doctrine in 1 Corinthians 15, where he specifies its modalities and importance for faith.
G0386.portee: The resurrection is the heart of Christian hope: it affirms that death is not the end, and that God will bring back to life those who believe in Jesus. The resurrection of Christ guarantees that of all believers (1 Corinthians 15:21-22). It is also an affirmation of divine justice: the resurrection to life or to judgment shows that God will repay each according to their works. This is why the apostles make the resurrection the heart of their proclamation and the unshakeable foundation of their courage.

sens: Stirring up a crowd, inciting them to revolt or sedition
Disturbing or disrupting a group through false teachings
G0387.detail:
1. The word describes the action of stirring up a crowd, exciting it to revolt. In Acts 17:6, Paul's adversaries accuse him of having troubled the entire city (the Segond says that Paul "has caused an uproar"). It is a political or civil agitation, a disturbance of public order through sedition.

2. The word also applies to those who disturb a Christian community through false doctrines. In Galatians 5:12, Paul speaks of those who trouble the believers by misleading them with bad teachings. Here, it is less about a physical revolt than about spiritual confusion.
G0387.origine: The word comes from two parts: "ana" (up, again) and "statoō" (to place, to establish). The basic image is that of a house or a life that is overturned, dislodged from its stability. The related Greek word "anastatos" means "without dwelling, uprooted." The verb thus expresses the idea of displacing someone from their position, destabilizing them deeply.
G0387.emploi: This verb appears three times in the New Testament, only in contexts of public or doctrinal trouble. In Acts 17:6, the crowd accuses Paul of troubling the whole city with his teachings. In Acts 21:38, the Roman tribune asks Paul if he is that Egyptian who caused a recent revolt and led four thousand brigands into the desert. In Galatians 5:12, Paul uses the same word to refer to those who sow trouble regarding circumcision among his churches: these are no longer political crowds, but false teachers who destabilize the faith of believers.
G0387.portee: This word reminds Christians that the word of God, when it is true, never seeks to trouble through lies or manipulation. It may certainly shake consciences through truth, but not through falsehood. It invites discernment: a teaching that troubles through lies is not from God. It is a call to vigilance against false teachers.

sens: Nail to a cross a second time
Treat with a contempt as grave as that inflicted during the crucifixion of Christ
Voluntarily renew the offense made to Jesus by the deliberate rejection of his sacrifice
G0388.detail:
1. The word literally evokes the action of nailing someone to a cross, repeated: the cross was the most terrible Roman punishment. In Hebrews 6:6, Paul does not imagine a real physical crucifixion, but the image is striking: those who abandon their faith after having known it treat Jesus with a contempt equivalent to that of the executioners.
2. One who "crucifies again" the Son of God through their apostasy (their abandonment of faith) imitates the gesture of Christ's enemies: they publicly reject him, "exposing him to disgrace," meaning they cover him with shame by openly denying him.
3. It is a voluntary and deliberate rejection of the redemptive sacrifice. The Greek word combines the prefix "ana" (again) and "stauroō" (to crucify), emphasizing that this act of renunciation renews the offense: it is not only to reject Christ, but to treat him as unworthy of any consideration.
G0388.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "ana" meaning "again" or "back," and the verb "stauroō" which comes from the Greek "stauros" (cross, stake). The cross was the pointed stake used for Roman crucifixion. By combining these elements, "anastauroō" literally expresses the action of nailing to a cross a second time. This verb belongs to the family of words designating the crucifixion, one of the darkest images of the New Testament.
G0388.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 6:6. Paul uses it to describe the grave sin of one who, after having tasted the goods of faith (the knowledge of Christ, the gifts of the Holy Spirit), turns away voluntarily. This is not an unconscious act or a momentary weakness: it is a conscious and obstinate rejection of the Lord. The context shows that Paul speaks of a complete apostasy, a deliberate turning away that makes repentance "impossible" (verse 4). The image of renewal — crucifying "again" — underscores the gravity of the act: these are not mere doubts or relapses, it is a renewed contempt for the one who gave his life.
G0388.portee: This word warns us against apostasy: to know Jesus and then reject him is to commit a grave spiritual crime, equivalent to the shedding of Christ's blood. For the believer, it invites vigilance: do not take salvation for granted, but remain faithful. It also reveals the height of the price paid by Jesus on the cross — a price so terrible that to renounce it voluntarily is described as crucifying him again. It is a call to honor, through persevering faith, the sacrifice of the Lord.

sens: To let out a deep sigh, a groan that comes from the heart
To express intense emotion through a sigh: sadness, fatigue, indignation, or distress
When speaking of Jesus, to manifest a spiritual reaction to unbelief or refusal to believe
G0389.detail:
1. The word describes the physical action of sighing intensely, letting out a groan from deep within the chest. It is a spontaneous act that reveals a profound emotional state.

2. This sigh expresses an overflowing emotion: whether it is sadness in the face of suffering, fatigue in a difficult situation, or indignation at the refusal to obey God. The sigh becomes a language of the heart.

3. In Mark 8:12, Jesus "sighs deeply in his spirit" when asked for a miraculous sign. This sigh reveals his spiritual dismay at a generation that refuses to believe and constantly demands proof, instead of trusting in God. It is the very heart of Jesus that is manifested at that moment.
G0389.origine: The word is composed of two parts: the prefix "ana-" (upward, back) and "stenazô" (to sigh, to groan). This composition intensifies the idea: a sigh that rises from the depths of being, a groan that truly comes from the heart. The simple verb "stenazô" appears elsewhere in the New Testament to express groans of distress or prayer.
G0389.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Mark 8:12, at a key moment when Jesus responds to the stubborn demand for a miraculous sign. This unique usage makes it a word loaded with meaning. Mark uses it to show that the refusal to believe deeply affects Jesus himself, beyond any fleeting reaction. It is a sigh that expresses incomprehension in the face of unbelief, a kind of spiritual complaint at the blindness of men.
G0389.portee: This word shows us that Jesus' emotions are not feigned or superficial: they spring from his heart. His sigh in the face of unbelief reminds us that the refusal to believe is not an abstract issue, but something that affects the very heart of God. This should encourage us to examine our own faith and not demand proof, but to surrender ourselves confidently to God.

sens: To overturn, to disturb something
To return, to go back to a place
To turn, to move here and there
To dwell, to stay in a place
To lead one's life, to behave, to act in a certain way
G0390.detail:
1. To overturn or disturb: the most concrete meaning of the word. John 2:15 illustrates this well: Jesus overturns the tables of the merchants in the Temple.
2. To return, to go back: to come back to a starting point or a previous state. Acts 5:22 and 15:16 use this sense of physical return or restoration.
3. To turn here and there, to move: the idea of movement that changes direction, of turning back on oneself.
4. To dwell, to stay: to remain in one place, to establish one's residence there. This is a nuance of the previous movement, when one settles there.
5. To lead one's life, to behave: this is the most common meaning in the New Testament epistles. It describes how someone lives on a daily basis, their actions, their moral behavior. In Ephesians 2:3, Paul says that Christians "formerly lived according to the desires of their flesh" — he speaks of their past way of life. In 2 Corinthians 1:12, Paul asserts that he has "conducted himself in the world" with holiness, meaning he acted with integrity. Similarly, in 1 Timothy 3:15, it is about how to "conduct oneself" in the Church.
G0390.origine: The Greek word ἀναστρέφω (anastrephō) combines the prefix ἀνα (ana, "upward, again") and στρέφω (strephō, "to turn"). The basic image is that of turning or turning back. In Hebrew, it mainly translates the verb שׁוּב (shoub), which means "to return, to go back." The Greek word plays on the idea of movement: one turns, one returns, then one establishes oneself, and finally one lives in a certain way. This progression from physical movement to moral behavior is typical of biblical Greek.
G0390.emploi: The verb appears nine times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles. In Acts (5:22 and 15:16), it retains the more concrete meaning of "to return" or "to go back." But from 2 Corinthians 1:12 onward, and especially in the pastoral epistles and the epistles of Peter, it takes on a moral and habitual sense: "to conduct oneself," "to live," "to lead one's life." The context shows that it refers to a persistent way of life, characteristic of the person. In Ephesians 2:3, the converts have changed their way of living; in 1 Timothy 3:15, the apostle teaches how believers should conduct themselves in the Church. This shift from movement to behavior reflects a biblical thought: how you move is how you behave, is how you live.
G0390.portee: This word invites the believer to realize that their life is not separate from their faith: it is a whole. The way one "conducts oneself," that is, how one acts every day, manifests what one truly is. The epistles use it to exhort Christians to conduct themselves in a manner worthy of Christ and consistent with their profession of faith. This reminds us that being a Christian is not an internal opinion, but a reality visible in actions.

sens: way of living, manner of acting and behaving on a daily basis
visible behavior that reflects character and convictions
the sum of acts and habits that mark a person in their relationship with others and with God
G0391.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the concrete manner in which someone lives day after day — how they act, speak, and conduct themselves towards others. Paul speaks of his own conduct in Judaism when he persecuted the Church (Galatians 1:13). 2. It is also the observable behavior, what is truly seen of someone. Timothy must be a model in conduct for the faithful (1 Timothy 4:12), and women can win their husbands without a word by their conduct (1 Peter 3:1). 3. More broadly, it encompasses the entirety of habits and practices of life, the way one exists. James calls for showing wisdom through good conduct (James 3:13), and Peter reminds that one was not redeemed from a futile way of life inherited from their forefathers, but for a new life (1 Peter 1:18).
G0391.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to turn" or "to walk," with the prefix "ana-" which reinforces the idea of movement. In later secular writings, it took on the figurative meaning of "way of living" or "manner of conducting oneself." The Bible uses it almost exclusively in the figurative sense: no longer physical movement, but the orientation of an entire life, how one "walks" in existence.
G0391.emploi: The word appears thirteen times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles of Peter and in Paul's correspondence. In Peter's letters (1 Peter and 2 Peter), it is frequent and often refers to Christian conduct that bears witness to non-believers or reflects holiness: "be holy in all your conduct" (1 Peter 1:15). In Paul's epistles, it evokes either a past conduct from which one turns away (Galatians 1:13: his former persecution), or a current testimony (Ephesians 4:22: putting off the old man with its practices). In James (3:13), conduct becomes the living proof of wisdom. The word always emphasizes that hidden life does not count: it is through our visible acts that our faith or character becomes real in the eyes of others.
G0391.portee: This word reminds the Christian that their faith is not only internal: it must be seen, lived, embodied in their daily gestures and habits. The "conduct" is the silent or speaking witness of what one truly believes. It can touch hearts closed to the word and convert without argument (1 Peter 3:1). This is why the apostles return to it constantly: good conduct is an act of obedience and love towards God, and a call to become holy in all of life.

sens: assemble scattered accounts to create a coherent narrative
methodically organize what has been gathered from memory
G0392.detail:
1. The word describes the action of gathering several separate stories or testimonies to unite them into a single coherent narrative. This is what Luke does when he "puts in order" the accounts of the life of Jesus that he has collected from those who have seen him (Luke 1:1): he does not juxtapose them randomly, but organizes them.
2. It is a work of formatting: one takes what one knows by hearsay or personal investigation, and arranges it logically and readably so that the reader understands and retains it.
G0392.origine: The word is formed from the prefix *ana-* ("again," "upward") and the verb *tassō* ("to arrange," "to set in place"). The image is one of arranging things in order, like putting objects on a shelf. It is a rare word in biblical Greek, used here to describe the literary work of composing a gospel.
G0392.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:1. Luke uses it to explain his method: he has investigated with eyewitnesses, he has gathered their testimonies, and he "puts them in order" to write his gospel. This verb shows that a gospel is not a mere collection, but a thoughtful composition where each element has its place.
G0392.portee: This word reminds us that the gospels are not raw recordings: they are works composed with care. Luke tells us that he investigates, that he seeks order and clarity. This invites us to trust the work of the biblical authors: they do not report haphazardly, but seek to convey the truth about Jesus in an intelligible and faithful manner.

sens: (of the sun, of light) appear on the horizon, shine
(of a plant, of a star) emerge, grow, appear
(figuratively) surge, emerge, become visible or manifest
(transitive) cause to appear, produce, engender
G0393.detail:
1. The most concrete and frequent meaning: the sun or light rising, showing itself on the horizon. In Matthew 5:45, God "makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good": the image evokes divine goodness shining indiscriminately on all. In Mark 16:2, the women come to the tomb "as the sun was rising": a moment of the day that marks a new beginning.
2. The appearance of what grows or emerges: a plant that sprouts, a star that shows itself in the sky. In Luke 12:54, a cloud "rises in the west," signaling rain. The image suggests something coming out of the horizon or out of the shadow.
3. In a figurative sense, the emergence of what becomes manifest or visible: the manifestation of a hidden reality. In Matthew 4:16, the light "has risen" on those sitting in darkness — this is revelation, salvation appearing. In Hebrews 7:14, the Lord "has risen" from the tribe of Judah: the appearance, the emergence of the Messiah in history.
4. Rarely, in the transitive mode: to cause to rise, to make appear, to produce. In Matthew 5:45, God "makes his sun rise" — God is the agent who produces this beneficial light.
G0393.origine: The Greek word combines ἀνά ("upward") and τέλλω ("to shine, to dawn"). The basic image is that of a light that rises, that emerges. In Hebrew, this verb translates several roots: צָמַח ("to sprout, to grow"), פָּרַח ("to bloom, to flourish") and זָרַח ("to shine, to glow"). These three images — sprouting, blooming, shining — converge in the idea of something that rises, that appears, that becomes visible for the first time.
G0393.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew and in the gospels. It primarily refers to the sun rising each morning: Matthew 13:6, Mark 4:6, Mark 16:2. It can also qualify light, a cloud, a star. But it never remains purely material: when Matthew applies this word to the light of Christ rising upon the people in darkness (4:16), or when Hebrews 7:14 says that the Lord has "risen" from Judah, the verb gains a spiritual and eschatological significance. It is the same act of emergence, of appearance, whether seen in the sky or in the history of salvation.
G0393.portee: This word invites us to recognize the appearance of God in our history as a dawn — both natural (the rising sun that nourishes every creature) and spiritual (the revelation that breaks the darkness). It reminds us that the presence of Christ, like the sun every morning, is certain, regular, and beneficial. For the believer, meditating on this verb is learning to see in the visible events of the world a sign of the invisible presence of the Lord who rises.

sens: Present something to someone for consideration
Highlight a topic of conversation
Submit a question or doctrine for examination by others
G0394.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to place before" or "to put under the eyes." It is the action of presenting something to someone in a direct and deliberate manner, as seen when Festus "exposes" Paul's case before King Agrippa, so that he may know and reflect on it (Acts 25:14).
2. The word also refers to putting a subject forward in conversation, stating it clearly before witnesses. Paul "exposes" the Gospel he preaches to the apostles in Jerusalem: he presents it to them in detail so that they may judge it, approve it, and to avoid any misunderstanding about his preaching (Galatians 2:2).
3. Implicitly, "to expose" suggests a serious intention: nothing is hidden, one lays all cards on the table before the relevant people. It is an act of honesty and transparency, whether done out of caution or respect.
G0394.origine: The Greek word is formed from the prefix "ana" (upward, forward) and the verb "titthēmi" (to place, to put). The basic image is that of "placing before oneself" or "putting forward." It is a compound verb that reinforces the idea of voluntary and public presentation. In classical and late Greek, it takes on the meaning of "to report," "to declare." In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew "haram," which means "to consecrate" or "to devote to destruction," but the Greek meaning leans more towards putting forward a question or a matter.
G0394.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, always in the middle voice (reflexive form) and in the sense of "to put forward," "to expose." In Acts 25:14, Festus, a Roman governor, uses it to say that he has presented the case of the prisoner Paul to King Agrippa, as a matter to be examined. In Galatians 2:2, Paul uses it to recount how he submitted the Gospel to the important apostles in Jerusalem. Both occurrences share the idea of presenting something important before the right people, in a context where clarity, mutual recognition, or approval is at stake.
G0394.portee: This word invites the Christian to transparency and honesty in their relationships: to expose their faith, convictions, or questions to others, without ulterior motives. It is also the image of the apostle who has nothing to hide, who submits his message to fraternal verification. For anyone teaching or influencing others, it reminds us of the importance of submitting one's teaching to the judgment of the brethren, rather than defending it in secret.

sens: The cardinal point where the sun rises
The direction or region located to the east
The appearance or rising (of the sun, of light)
G0395.detail:
1. The east is the cardinal point marked by the rising of the sun: it is the direction where the celestial body appears each morning. In Matthew 2:1 and 2:2, the Magi come from the east, having traveled from the lands of western Asia (Persia, Arabia) where the sun rises in relation to Jerusalem.
2. By extension, the word simply designates the region of the east or the geographical east. In Matthew 24:27, lightning flashes from the east to the west to describe a movement from east to west.
3. In Luke 1:78, "the rising sun" translates the same Greek word and signifies the act of rising, the dawn — here the messianic light that "has visited us from on high." It conveys the sense of radiance and sudden appearance.
G0395.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀνατέλλω (to rise, to appear), composed of ἀνά (upward) and τέλλω (to accomplish, to make appear). Its basic image is that of upward movement: the sun rising on the horizon. In Hebrew, this word generally translates מִזְרָח (mizrah) or קָדִים (qadim), both meaning "east" or "eastward," with the idea of rising or that which comes from before (the initial direction).
G0395.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew (six occurrences) and in Revelation. In Matthew 2, it designates the region from which the Magi arrive following the star: it is a geographical and concrete sense. In Matthew 8:11 and 24:27, it retains this sense of cardinal direction (east and west mark the ends of the known world). In Luke 1:78, the Christological context transforms the meaning: "the rising sun" is no longer simply a celestial phenomenon, but the image of the coming of Christ who illuminates the darkness. Revelation uses the term to locate the gates of the heavenly temple (21:13) and the kings coming from the east (16:12), remaining within the geographical sense.
G0395.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible speaks the language of men: it uses visible and everyday realities (the rising sun) to evoke spiritual realities (the coming of Christ, the light of God). For the believer, the east becomes a symbol of renewal and hope — each sunrise evokes Christ coming to illuminate us with His grace. The Magi following the star from the east show how the light of Christ draws distant peoples to Him.

sens: To make something fall by pushing or striking it
To destroy, annihilate a structure or system
To deeply disturb, shake someone's conviction or stability
G0396.detail:
1. The most concrete sense is physical: to overturn material objects. Jesus overturns the tables of the money changers in the temple (John 2:15), a violent gesture that destroys the established order. It is the whip that acts, pushing things down.
2. The word can mean to completely destroy or annihilate a building, an institution, an established truth. This is the sense of "destruction" or "abolition."
3. In a figurative sense, to overturn faith or to overturn families (2 Timothy 2:18; Titus 1:11) means to shake, undermine convictions, disrupt moral and familial order. False teachers overturn the faith of some Christians by teaching lies about the resurrection. It is an internal overturning: it troubles minds and hearts.
G0396.origine: The Greek word is composed of ἀνα- (ana-, "upward, backward") and τρέπω (trepō, "to turn, to direct"). The basic image is that of twisting, turning over: to make something turn upside down, to project it backward. In Hebrew, the word often corresponds to דָּחָה (dāḥāh, "to push away") or הָדַף (hādaph, "to drive away"), which also evoke the violent movement of rejection.
G0396.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament. John 2:15 describes the concrete action of Jesus overturning the tables of the temple: a physical, direct, visible act. In 2 Timothy 2:18 and Titus 1:11, the meaning becomes abstract: to overturn is no longer a bodily gesture, but an effect in the spirit and morality. False teachers overturn faith (doctrinal certainty) or families (domestic and spiritual order). The context changes the tone: from the just action of Christ to the danger of heresies that destabilize the Church.
G0396.portee: This word reveals two aspects of overturning: that which Christ performs (purifying the temple, restoring true order) and that which false doctrines produce (destroying faith, disrupting lives). For the believer, it invites discernment: what overturns legitimately and what destroys illegitimately? It is a word of warning against influences that seek to shake confidence in the Gospel and the stability of the Christian community.

sens: To feed and care for a child from birth
To take in a child and care for them as a son or daughter
To train someone through instruction and education
G0397.detail:
1. To feed and care for a child from birth: this is the daily material care of a baby or young child. This is how Pharaoh's daughter nursed Moses during his early months (Acts 7:20).
2. To take in a child and care for them as a son or daughter: this is the welcoming and integration into a family, not just feeding. When Pharaoh's daughter found little Moses, she took him in and raised him as her own child, despite his different origins (Acts 7:21).
3. To train someone through instruction and education: this is developing a person's intelligence and character through teaching. Paul was nurtured in Jerusalem under the teaching of the master Gamaliel, learning the Law in detail (Acts 22:3).
G0397.origine: The word ἀνατρέφω is formed from the prefix ἀνα- ("upward," "again") and the verb τρέφω ("to nourish"). This combination suggests the idea of "nourishing while developing," of making someone grow by providing what is necessary. The root τρέφω primarily evokes the material action of providing food, but ἀνατρέφω gradually expands to include complete education — the care of both body and spirit.
G0397.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always in Acts, and each time it speaks of a person being taken in and raised from childhood to adulthood. With Moses (Acts 7:20-21), it emphasizes Pharaoh's daughter's personal commitment: not only did she nourish him, but she adopted him. With Paul (Acts 22:3), the word no longer speaks of nourishment, but of strict education in the Torah under a great teacher. Thus, the meaning shifts from the physical care of a small child to the intellectual and moral formation of a young man, while retaining the central idea: someone takes charge of the complete development of another person.
G0397.portee: This word reminds us that education is a commitment of love and responsibility towards the younger ones. For the Christian, it emphasizes the importance of transmitting not only knowledge but also values and a living relationship with God. The example of Paul trained by Gamaliel and that of Moses raised as Pharaoh's son show how God uses teachers and families to prepare His servants, even in environments that do not yet belong to Him.

sens: To become visible, to show visually
To emerge, to become visible
To manifest, to appear clearly
G0398.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is "to appear to the sight": when one sees something showing up on the horizon or becoming known through vision. In Acts 21:3, Paul and his companions "saw the island of Cyprus" as it emerged: the ship sailing suddenly brings Cyprus into view for the travelers.
2. In a figurative sense, the word means "to manifest" or "to appear clearly." In Luke 19:11, Jesus speaks of the kingdom of God that will "appear": the disciples believe that the reign of God will manifest immediately, becoming visible and real before their eyes.
3. The word carries the idea of a revelation: what was hidden or distant suddenly becomes present and manifest to the one who looks or to whom it is announced.
G0398.origine: The Greek word is formed from the prefix "ana-" (upward, forward) and "phainō" (to show, to shine, to illuminate). The starting image is that of light: to shine upward is to illuminate, to reveal. The root connects to the idea of appearance and visible manifestation. In Hebrew, this verb often translates the word צָדַק "to be just" or "to become manifest" in its active form.
G0398.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament according to the provided usages. First in the passive sense in Luke 19:11, where the kingdom of God is expected as something that will "appear" or "manifest." Then in Acts 21:3 in the active sense (past participle), where "having seen" Cyprus means that the island becomes visible to the sailors. In both cases, it is a manifestation or sudden appearance: either to physical sight (the island) or to consciousness or expectation (the kingdom).
G0398.portee: This word reminds us that the kingdom of God is not a distant abstraction, but a reality that must manifest, become visible and tangible. For the believer, it evokes the importance of remaining attentive to the presence and action of God that progressively reveals itself in history and in life.

sens: To lead or bring upward, ascending
To present a sacrifice at the altar, to offer to God
To bear, to endure
G0399.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of movement: to lead someone or something upward, to a high place. Jesus "leads" his disciples up a high mountain (Matthew 17:1, Mark 9:2), and at the moment of his ascension, he is "taken up" to heaven (Luke 24:51). It is a physical movement upward.

2. In a religious context, it is to bring a sacrifice to the altar to offer to God. The priests "offer" sacrifices (Hebrews 7:27), and the Church "offers" to God a sacrifice of praise (Hebrews 13:15). This meaning extends the physical movement to the idea of presenting something to God with respect and adoration.

3. Finally, the word can mean to bear or endure, particularly in the expression "to bear sins": Christ "offered himself" and bears the sins of many (Hebrews 9:28), meaning he endures and takes them upon himself (see also 1 Peter 2:24 where sins are "borne" on the wood of the cross).
G0399.origine: The word is composed of "ana" (upward, ascending) and "pherō" (to bear, to carry). In Greek, this combination first evokes a physical movement upward. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it primarily translates the Hebrew verb "alah" (to ascend, to offer) and sometimes "qatar" (to burn, to offer as a sacrifice). This family of words expresses the idea of presenting something upward, or carrying it while ascending.
G0399.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles (Hebrews, 1 Peter, James). In Matthew and Mark, it simply describes the action of leading someone upward (the disciples to the mountain). In Luke, it refers to the ascension of Christ. In Hebrews and 1 Peter, the context becomes sacrificial and spiritual: one "offers" sacrifices, praise, and ultimately Christ "bears" or "offers" himself. Everywhere, the word retains this notion of movement upward or toward God, from the concrete to the spiritual.
G0399.portee: This word teaches us that our worship and offerings are never insignificant: they "rise" to God, carried by Christ. It also reminds us that Christ, in ascending to the cross and offering himself as a sacrifice, did not merely accomplish an action; he "bore" our sins—a burden he took upon himself for us. For the Christian, it is an invitation to "offer" one's life, praise, and actions to God, aware that all that rises to him passes through Christ.
